en: The *Sphuṭārthā* Commentary on the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, composed by the master Haribhadra as a treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The First Chapter: The Omniscience of All Aspects.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Auspicious Invocation.
Homage to that Prajñāpāramitā for whose sake this commentary on the *Alaṃkāra-kārikās* is composed for the purpose of [elucidating] all its ornaments. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 0.1)
Having heard that great treatise from the Lord Ajita, the Protector Ārya-Asaṅga, through his attachment to the world [and] his devotion to the Saṅgha, divided it. Abhisamayālaṃkāra 0.2.

Then Vasubandhu, a kinsman devoted to the welfare of the world, relying upon his own mental continuum and the internal objects of knowledge, composed this commentary on that [work]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 0.3)

Seeing that liberation, which was composed by him who is renowned as one included within the Noble Assembly, appeared as if it were uncomposed, he produced another [commentary] with a mind of middle capacity. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 0.4)
Then, although he had not mastered the treatises in their entirety and remained at the stage of faith, Vimuktisena provided an exposition according to his own insight. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 0.5)
When this has been thus proclaimed by the best of the learned, if even the slightest deficiency were perceived, everything here would be incomplete;
yet in this [work], everything is perfectly accomplished, causing great wonder. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 0.6)

This path is extremely difficult to find, profound, and true to reality; it has been attained through the compassion of the Buddhas and must be thoroughly investigated by the wise. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 0.7)
In every respect, I have no domain at all; nevertheless, I venture forth because it is conducive to the practice of merit and out of a desire to bring benefit to myself and others.

The noble Maitreya, demonstrating his own adherence to virtuous conduct, and having determined through his own unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) that faith alone regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the primary cause for attaining all that is most excellent,

spoke as follows at the outset in order to inspire faith so as to set forth the Blessed Mother— who is a mine of supreme, unsurpassed, and infinite jewels of qualities— preceded by a description of her qualities according to how they truly are: [He] pays homage to the Mother.
That which, through omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), leads the Śrāvakas seeking peace to tranquility;
that which, through knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), accomplishes the welfare of the world for those who act for the benefit of beings;
and endowed with which, the Sages proclaim this entire universe in all its aspects—[that is the Perfection of Wisdom].
Homage to that Mother of the Buddha, who possesses a host of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas. Abhis_1.1 //
By this verse, its possession of extraordinary greatness is proclaimed.
Having heard that, those who follow through faith (śraddhānusārin) will, without doubt, soon produce faith in it.

Those who follow through the Dharma (dharmānusārin), by means of such valid cognition (pramāṇa) as "because it is devoid of a single or multiple nature," [will likewise produce faith] in the Mother, whose characteristic is the meaning of the verse regarding the thorough knowledge of the aspect of the path—the entity that is unarisen.

Having ascertained that the Perfection of Wisdom— which consists of the three natures of the three types of omniscience and is the creator of the Buddhas and others— is necessarily existent because no contradiction is perceived, they generate faith toward it.
Through faith in it, both kinds of persons, desiring its qualities, respect it in every way and to the utmost degree for the sake of upholding the various teachings based upon it and so forth.
Then, through the sequence of generating the wisdoms beginning with that consisting of hearing, they attain supreme excellence.
For this very reason, in the *Bhagavatī*, fervent application (*pradāsa*) alone is the cause for attaining all supreme excellence.
In that regard, the eight topics are subsumed within the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Keeping in mind that all goals will be accomplished through these [three types of omniscience] according to the method to be explained, he praises the Perfection of Wisdom by means of the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*).
The Śrāvaka—who is included within that category—and the Pratyekabuddha, who is taught as following a single stage and is slightly superior in terms of liberation, both desire Nirvāṇa.

That [Perfection of Wisdom], which brings about the two kinds of Nirvāṇa characterized by the presence or absence of the substratum (*sopadhi-nirupadhi*), consists in the non-arising of the knowledge of all things.

Homage to that Mother who gives birth to the Buddhas— who, surrounded by a retinue of Śrāvakas and others, are the masters of supreme yoga whose bodies are restrained and who, through their union with the non-arisen *sarvākārajñatā*, set in motion in every way the wheels of Dharma that counteract all conduct— those Bodhisattvas who act for the welfare of the world throughout the duration of *saṃsāra* and who accomplish the aims of all people through the non-arisen *sarvamārgajñatā*.

Thus, when the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-śāstra*— preceded by salutation and praise— subsumes [the teachings] under one or another of the categories of entities (*vastu*), antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), or aspects (*ākāra*),
there is first of all the futility of laboring over its meaning in the first category.
For indeed, there is no collection of entities here in the *Prajñāpāramitā* that has not been previously stated in the treatises on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
In the second [case], because it includes only the bases of purification (*vyavadāna-vastu*) and excludes the bases of affliction (*sāṃkleśika-vastu*), it is not known of what this is the antidote.

In the third, because it includes only the mere aspects (*ākāra*) devoid of a basis (*nirvastuka*), nothing at all has been stated here regarding the realization of the object; thus, the labor of composing the treatise would be entirely in vain.
If it is asked, "Why will others not suspect this?"— it is not so,

because by means of the inclusion of all the realizations (*abhisamaya*) within the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*) of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Unsurpassed Buddhas respectively, all three categories are indeed subsumed.
As it is said in the *Madhyamaka-jinajananyā*: "Subhūti, the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) belongs to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*) belongs to the Bodhisattvas; and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) belongs to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas."
"Blessed One, for what reason is there omniscience for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
"Subhūti, it is because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know exactly as many external and internal phenomena as there are."
But it is not by way of the path,
nor even in all its aspects;
therefore, omniscience belongs to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"Blessed One, for what purpose is the knowledge of the path for Bodhisattvas?
"Subhūti, it is because the path of the Śrāvaka [is to be known] by Bodhisattvas."
Whatever is the path of a pratyekabuddha and whatever is the path of a Buddha— all these paths are produced and known;
they too are brought to fulfillment.
The activities of those paths are also carried out until the fulfillment of their vows and the ripening of sentient beings.
Or, as long as the purification of the buddha-field is being performed, they have not yet realized the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) correctly;
therefore, the knowledge of the path (mārgajñatā) belongs to the bodhisattvas.
"Blessed One, for what reason is there omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha?
"Subhūti, it is by whatever aspect (*ākāra*) and by whatever characteristic (*liṅga*)."

The Tathāgatas understand that sign, that characteristic, and that cause by which phenomena are manifested; therefore, this is the "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha.
"Thus, even in this concise [Prajñāpāramitā]—the Mother of the Victors—it says: 'Even one who wishes to train in the Śrāvaka-bhūmi,' and so forth;
yet it is also stated in full detail in the extensive version."
In this regard, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) has as its basis the impermanence and so forth of phenomena such as form, and has as its fruit the abandonment of delusion regarding a self (*ātmamoha*).

Knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) has as its basis the departure via all vehicles through the non-direct realization of reality, and has as its fruits the gathering of beings not yet gathered and so forth.

Omniscience in all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) has as its basis the non-arising of all phenomena, has as its fruit the welfare of sentient beings that is uninterrupted and extends to the limits of the realm of space, and consists in the abandonment of the reconnection of latent predispositions (*vāsanā-pratisandhi*) through the realization of the limit of existence (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Thus, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the exposition of all realizations has been completed by way of summarizing the aspects that serve as the antidotes to all objective entities; this is established. As for the purpose of undertaking this treatise:

it is for those of dull intellect who [find difficulty] with the extensive, medium, and concise Mother [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras]—[that is, those who find difficulty with the concise, medium, and extensive versions].

Since the sequence of the eight realizations (*aṣṭābhisamaya*), which contains the entire meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, was already taught by the Compassionate One out of a desire for the welfare of beings endowed with faith, one might wonder: "What is the purpose of the Blessed Noble Ajita’s demonstration of it? In order to dispel this doubt and to generate interest, [the author] speaks, demonstrating the factors for engagement—including the relationship (*sambandha*) inherent within the purpose of the purpose of the subject matter of his own treatise: [The verse: "The Victorious One, having attained the state of omniscience, taught the Mother of the Victors; Ajita, desiring to explain her meaning, composed this treatise. The wise should behold that path to omniscience which has been taught here by the Teacher, as it is untouched by others. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.2)

And having established the meaning of the Sūtra within their memory, [the author] intends that they may practice the tenfold course of Dharma with ease; this is the purpose of the undertaking. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.3)
Thus, since omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) alone is the path to Buddhahood, it is the primary focus because it serves as the defining characteristic of all the realizations (*abhisamaya*).

The subject matter taught by the Blessed One— the instructor of all beings through the three miracles— in the three Mother Scriptures of the Victor is interconnected in the form of the expression and the expressed, the means and the goal, and the practice.

When it has been well established that [the path] is untouched by those who have not practiced the selflessness of all phenomena—such as those who are free from passion for external objects or internal states—and who have not reached it through the sequence of wisdom consisting of hearing and so forth; and when one has correctly taken up the meaning of the entire *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, which consist of the eight clear realizations (*aṣṭābhisamaya*) and the practice of the application of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and generosity; then, by way of the sequence of realizations beginning with the "Joyful" stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which is characterized by the realization of the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

"One should realize [the Perfection of Wisdom] in all its aspects" is for the sake of the purpose of the purpose; it is the purpose of commencing the treatise so that those to be trained may easily practice the characteristics of the desired Perfection of Wisdom, the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), the application, and so forth.

Having thus explained the connection and other introductory elements of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and observing that it facilitates ease of exposition by ensuring that the meaning of the treatise— though already well-differentiated— is not confused for the sake of the easy practice of those to be trained, [the author] proceeds with a concise and detailed exposition by means of fifteen verses.
He states the physical establishment of the *prajñāpāramitā*:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed through eight categories of meaning:
omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and thereafter, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.4)
Complete awakening in all its aspects, the culmination, the serial, the momentary awakening in a single instant, and the Dharma-body—these are your eight [forms]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.5)
The generation of the thought of enlightenment, instruction, the fourfold limb of penetration, and the basis of practice, which has the dharmadhātu as its intrinsic nature. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.6)

The objective support, the aim, the acts of donning armor and setting out, the accumulations together with the departure—all these constitute the omniscience of all aspects belonging to the Sage. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.7)

The path of seeing, which possesses great benefits through its worldly and transcendent qualities, includes the turning [of the world] dark-blue and so forth, as well as the two paths of the disciple and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha]. Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.8.
Activity, resolute belief, and those [states] praised, extolled, and lauded;
the two mental orientations regarding dedication and sympathetic joy are unsurpassed. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.9)
Accomplishment and ultimate purity—this is the path of cultivation for wise Bodhisattvas; thus is the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) proclaimed. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.10)
Through wisdom there is no abiding in existence; through compassion there is no staying in peace.
Without skillful means there is remoteness, and with skillful means there is proximity.

The path of seeing of the Śrāvakas and others is held to be omniscience (sarvajñatā) insofar as it consists of the discordant factors and their antidotes, the application, and its equality. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.12)

The aspects together with their applications, the qualities and faults along with their characteristics, the stages conducive to liberation and penetration, the learner, and the irreversible assembly. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.13)
The equality of existence and peace, supreme purification of the field, and the complete awakening in all its aspects—this is [the path] together with skill in means. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.14)
Its sign, its increase, its firm establishment, and the stability of the mind;
thus, the fourfold counteragent to conceptual construction is of four kinds. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.15)
On each of the two paths called "seeing" and "cultivation," there is the immediate concentration (ānantarya-samādhi) together with the opposing errors.
The realization of the summit is threefold, as is the gradual [realization];
the realization in a single moment is fourfold by way of its characteristics. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 1.17.
The essential body, that which is with enjoyment, that which leads to liberation, and likewise another;
the Dharma-body, together with its activity, is thus proclaimed as fourfold.

Thus, in that regard, there is a concise exposition through the inclusion of eight topics in the first two verses; thereafter, a detailed explanation follows by summarizing the meaning of those very same topics through thirteen verses. In this way, it is a "well-spoken" (subhāṣita) work because it is taught both in brief and in detail.

Since these summary verses (*piṇḍārthakārikā*) themselves will be explained by the entire treatise to be composed by the author of the work— beginning with "The production of the thought [of awakening] for the sake of others"—
the author, intending that their explanation would be provided precisely through that [subsequent] explanation, did not explain them here for fear of excessive prolixity (*vīpsā*).
[Now begins the section on] the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Having thus explained the summarized meaning of the entire [work] as "the production of the thought of enlightenment" (cittotpāda), and since those bodhisattvas who desire to attain awakening must realize the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) because it is the resultant state,
[the author], wishing now to explain the verse summarizing the knowledge of all aspects, states the essential nature of the production of the thought of enlightenment together with its object:

The production of the thought of enlightenment (cittotpāda) is the desire for perfect awakening (samyaksambodhi) for the sake of others. Having become a Buddha, one should exert effort toward the welfare of others according to their capacity; thus, the production of the thought of enlightenment is twofold, characterized by the aspiration and the venturing forth, having the nature of the desire for perfect awakening for the sake of others. This desire for perfect awakening is a mental factor (caitasika), which is the wholesome zeal for the Dharma (kuśala-dharmacchanda) consisting of that very prayer.
If the mind that arises as a manifestation of a specific object is "the arising of the mind" (*cittotpāda*), how could that [mental factor] be the arising of the mind?
This is true.
However, since the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) arises when there is aspiration characterized by a longing for wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma),

the effect is here indicated by its cause; furthermore, this figurative usage is employed to make known that all wholesome qualities increase for the bodhisattva who thus aspires— thus there is no fault.

The generation of the mind (cittotpāda) accompanied by the aspiration for perfect enlightenment—whether that aspiration or prayer takes another form or is the desire for perfect enlightenment—is extended [to this case] by means of the prayer;
or rather, it is for the purpose of making known that "this mind arises together with such an aspiration."
If it is asked: "What is this perfect enlightenment?

And what is the welfare of others, characterized by the desire for which and for the sake of which the production of the thought [of awakening] occurs? It is said: "That [enlightenment] and that [welfare] are stated both in brief and in detail, according to the Sūtra. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.19)

By means of the statement intended to demonstrate that one should practice this perfection of wisdom— intended to make known that in all three Mothers of the Jinas, as well as in the perfection of wisdom and in [the perfections of] giving and so forth, there is the non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient— and intended to show that one who wishes to establish all sentient beings according to their capacity in nirvāṇa, and those who are stingy in giving and so forth, should practice this perfection of wisdom.
In accordance with the meaning of the sūtras, both in brief and in detail, perfect enlightenment for the sake of others has been explained.

Thus, "the production of the thought of awakening is the desire for perfect enlightenment for the sake of others" should be understood. Although everything has been stated on this occasion of explaining the intended meaning of the entire treatise in all its aspects, much more remains to be said; therefore, [it is not discussed here] primarily.
Thus, having described the nature of the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) as having an object, he now states its twenty-two divisions in two intermediate verses:
"By means of earth, gold, moon, and fire; by treasure, jewel-mine, and ocean..."
By means of the Vajra, Acala, medicinal herbs, and friends, as well as the wish-fulfilling gem, the sun, and songs. // Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.20 //

And that [benefit] is of twenty-two kinds, consisting of the waters from the king’s treasury, the great highways, vehicles, and flowing springs, as well as the rivers and clouds of words of joy. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.21)

(The production of the thought of awakening) is accompanied by: zeal, intention, resolute intention, application, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, knowledge, supernormal knowledges, merit, gnosis, qualities conducive to the factors of enlightenment, compassion, insight, mnemonic formulas, eloquence, the festival of the Dharma, the single vehicle, and the Dharma-body.

Respectively, they are similar to the earth, fine gold, the white fortnight, a forest, the moon, a blazing fire, a great treasure, a mine of jewels, the great ocean, the king of mountains (Vajraparvatarāja), medicine, a spiritual friend, a wish-fulfilling gem, the sun, the sweet chanting of the Dharma, a great king, a granary, a great highway, a vehicle, spring water, joyful speech, the continuous flow of a river, and clouds;
because they serve as the foundation for all pure dharmas.
Because it is unchanging until the limit of enlightenment, because it proceeds toward the increase of all pure dharmas,
and because it burns the fuel of the obscurations to the three types of omniscience.
Because it satisfies all sentient beings, because it serves as the locus for the jewels of virtuous qualities,
and because it is unshakable by the occurrence of any undesirable calamities.
Because it is indivisible due to the firmness of conviction,
because it is unshakable by distraction from the object of focus,
and because it pacifies the diseases of the afflictive obscurations and the obscurations to knowledge.
Because of not abandoning the welfare of sentient beings in any state,
because of the fulfillment of the fruit according to one's vow,
and because of bringing the people to be trained to maturity.
Because he teaches the Dharma that captivates those to be trained;
because he accomplishes the welfare of others through unimpeded power;
and because he is the locus for the treasury of the vast accumulations of merit and wisdom.
Because it follows the path traversed by all noble ones;
because it provides a comfortable conveyance by avoiding falling into either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
and because it is inexhaustible through the retention of the Dharma, whether heard or not yet heard.
It is [respectively] so called because it causes those disciples who desire liberation to hear what is pleasing;
because it is unconfused due to its performance of the welfare of others;
and because it is suitable for manifesting such things as dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven. Thus it occurs in accordance with their respective order.
Thus, twenty-two productions of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) have been explained by means of [the similes] "earth," "gold," "moon," "fire," and so forth.
Among these, the first three—being respectively weak, middling, and intense—are included within the stage of the beginner (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*).
Following that, one is included within the path of entry into the first bhūmi.
Following that, there are ten [mental states] subsumed under the ten stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā), which have as their domain the paths of seeing and cultivation;
after those, five are subsumed under the path of distinction.
Following that, three productions of the thought of enlightenment are subsumed under the Buddha-stage by way of the preparatory, fundamental, and concluding phases.

Thus ends the classification of the generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), which is subsumed from the stage of the beginner up to the stage of a Buddha. 2. Instruction (*avavāda*) as it arises in connection [with the generation of the mind].

Having explained the divisions [of the instruction], the *avavāda* (instruction) is the teaching for the sake of establishing the dharmas implied by that [instruction]—for a bodhisattva who has generated the initial and subsequent *bodhicitta* at the appropriate time, who has requested the object of his desire, the generation of *bodhicitta*, and who seeks the preservation of attained qualities and their further increase. Therefore, he says:
"And regarding practice, and regarding the truths, and regarding the three jewels beginning with the Buddha..."
In non-attachment, in tirelessness, and in the complete grasping of the path. // Abhis. 1.22 //
It should be known that within the five eyes, the six qualities of the superknowledges, and the paths of seeing and cultivation, there is the tenfold instruction. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.23)

Instruction on practice (*pratipatty-avavāda*) is the teaching that one should engage in the practice of the bodhicitta according to its aforementioned divisions by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), being uncommon to the Śrāvakas and others, and without transgressing the conventional and ultimate truths.

Regarding suffering (*duḥkha*): because both emptiness—the nature of form and so forth as the result—and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are of the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), they are of a single essence.

Regarding origin (*samudaya*): since emptiness is not distinct from form and so forth which serve as its causes, form and so forth do not possess the properties of arising, ceasing, affliction, or purification.

Regarding cessation (*nirodha*)—which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) devoid of arising, ceasing, affliction, purification, decrease, increase, and so forth—it is taught that there is no form, up to and including no ignorance, no arising of ignorance, no cessation of ignorance, no Buddha, and no awakening.

Regarding the path (*mārga*), it is the instruction that through the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as giving, one practices by way of the non-connection and non-disconnection of the internal emptinesses and so forth with the external emptinesses and so forth, as well as with the prior and subsequent limits;
this is the instruction on the truths (*satyāvavāda*).

Regarding the Buddha: because the Buddha and awakening are characterized by oneness, there is the knowledge of the equality of the object and the subject through the non-apprehension of the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is the characteristic of the qualities that constitute a Buddha, by way of not associating it with form and so forth. Regarding the Dharma: it is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena that are subsumed within the three types of omniscience, through the inclusion of the aspects that serve as the antidotes to all entities.

Regarding the Saṅgha: because it is included within the Jewel of the Buddha, [this knowledge arises] regarding the seven [members], distinguished by those established in the fruits and those entering toward them, excluding the Arhat.

The instruction on the Three Jewels (*ratnatrayāvavāda*) is the teaching that there is activity through non-arising (*anutpādatā*) among the Great Beings— namely, the Pratyekabuddhas together with the eight types [of Śrāvakas] distinguished by dull faculties and so forth, and the twenty-fold number of noble, irreversible Bodhisattvas in training (*śaikṣa*).

Because one might have an attachment to the body and so forth as being a source of pleasure toward the practice of the aforementioned goal due to having initiated vigor (*ārabdhavīryatā*), the instruction on non-attachment (*asakti*) is the teaching that the body and so forth lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*).

If the desired goal is not accomplished even through practice over a very long period of time, one who is prone to fear might become weary; therefore, instruction and advice regarding non-exhaustion consists in the non-conceptualization of everything from form up to perfect enlightenment. If, while receiving instruction on the path from the Buddhas and others residing in the ten directions for each specific purpose, the mind were to become discouraged, then instruction regarding the full undertaking of the path consists in training in the fact that all phenomena are by nature unborn.

The instruction on the five eyes is the training in the realization that the five eyes— the flesh eye, the ripening divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye— which have respectively as their objects specific things, the death and rebirth of all sentient beings, the non-conceptualization of all phenomena, the realization of all noble persons, and the perfect awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects, are one in their suchness (*tathatā*).

The instruction on the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñāvavāda*) is the realization of the primordial quiescence of the superknowledges— namely, the superknowledge of miraculous powers, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of former abodes, the divinely produced divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows— which have as their functions the shaking of the earth and so forth, hearing even the most subtle sounds throughout all world-systems, fully knowing the minds of others such as whether they are with passion or not, recollecting one's own and others' many previous births, seeing all forms, and the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.

The instruction on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is taught as follows: the yogi meditates upon the path of seeing—which consists of the nature of sixteen moments subsumed within the four truths, and which is composed of the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of dharma and subsequent cognition—as being non-attached in all respects, like a magician whose form is not fixed anywhere due to the realization that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; he does so because it serves as the antidote to the things that are to be abandoned. This is the teaching on the instruction for the path of seeing.

Just as the designation of the conditioned and the unconditioned as being mutually inseparable due to their single nature, so too there is no distinction between the paths of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because they take as their object that reality which has been brought face-to-face by the aforementioned path of seeing. Thus, the formal establishment of a "path of cultivation" is not based on its specific characteristics; nevertheless, it is cultivated as the antidote to the objects to be abandoned, by way of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*).
The instruction on the paths of teaching and cultivation is as follows: regarding the perfection of wisdom, which is the intrinsic nature of the dharmas produced by that bodhicitta,
the practice characterized by non-apprehension has as its objective support the four noble truths.
That which is the basis for the three refuges,
that which is non-attachment as the cause for proceeding toward excellence,
and that which is weariness as the cause for not turning back from proceeding;
That which is the cause for not departing for another vehicle is the thorough grasping of the practice; that which is the cause for not being led by others is the five eyes;
and that which is the cause for the fulfillment of the knowledge of all aspects is the six superknowledges.

The two causes of finality—the paths of seeing and cultivation—all of that has been indicated in the section on instruction; since the entire purpose is accomplished by this much alone, there are ten kinds of instruction.
Regarding the section on the Jewel of the Saṅgha, he says there are two intermediate verses for the sake of easy understanding:

Those with dull or sharp faculties, those who have attained through faith or through vision, those who go from family to family, those with one interval, those who attain nirvāṇa in the intermediate state, those who attain it upon being reborn, those who attain it with effort, those who attain it without effort, and those who go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.24)
The three types of leapers, those for whom existence is at its peak, those who have abandoned attachment to the form realm,
those who attain peace in this very life, the body-witness, and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha]— these are the twenty.

Based on the path of seeing consisting of sixteen moments, which is comprised within the *mārgajñatā* to be explained hereafter, there are two types of those entering the first fruit, distinguished as followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and followers by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Following that is the stream-enterer (*srota-āpanna*).
Then, that same person is further divided into two other types based on being of "noble family" among gods or humans (*deva-manuṣya-kulaṃkula*).

Then there is the one who has entered the path toward the second fruit, who possesses either dull or sharp faculties and is characterized as either "attained through faith" or "attained through vision.
Following that is the once-returner;
then there is another, the one who has only one interval remaining.
The one who has entered upon the third fruit is, as before, either one who has attained through faith or one who has attained through vision.

From there, the non-returner is of four types: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains it upon rebirth, one who attains it with exertion, and one who attains it without exertion.

First, there are three types of those who have ascended to the higher realms (*ūrdhvāvakrānta*): one who goes to Akaniṣṭha, one who performs a "leap" (*pluta*), and one who dies in all places (*sarvasthānacyuta*).

Then, there are two other types: one who has reached the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and is free from passion for the realm of form (*rūpavītarāga*), being one who attains peace in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmapraśama*) and a bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*).
Finally, there is the one practicing for the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).
Then there are twenty [stages] regarding the Pratyekabuddha.
Regarding the "limbs of penetration" (*nirvedhāṅga*):
for one who has received instruction and is thus a beginner, there is the cultivation of the limbs of penetration; therefore, he speaks of the limbs of penetration.

For the sake of the noble ones who, according to their respective natures, engage with the fourfold conceptualization through its object, its aspect, its cause, and its thorough grasping, [the following is taught]. Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.26.
The superiority of the [levels of] heat and so forth—whether weak, medium, or intense—of the protecting Bodhisattva over the Śrāvakas who possess the sword [of the path], is established. Abhis 1.27.

Following the roots of merit characterized by faith and so forth—which constitute the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*)—and which have attained excellence through hearing and other means, there arise for Bodhisattvas the four mundane roots of merit consisting of cultivation (*laukikabhāvanāmaya*) that are conducive to the penetration of the Four Truths (*caturnirvedhabhāgīya*). These are: the root of merit called "having attained the heat" (*ūṣmagata*), and from that, "having attained the summit" (*mūrdhagata*).

From that, the stage of Patience (kṣānti) is attained, and from that, the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (agradharma); thus they arise in the sequence of weak and so forth. Alternatively, they are distinguished by the classification of individuals according to their faculties—such as those with weak faculties associated with Bodhisattvas—and by the specific aspects such as non-attachment, which serve as the antidotes to the vision of dharmas that take the Four Truths as their object, consisting of entities distinguished by weak, medium, and intense objects as will be explained.

Due to the distinction of being the cause for the realization of the three vehicles, and because they are fully embraced by skillful means and spiritual friends, the four conceptualizations of subject and object—which are to be abandoned through the paths of seeing and meditation—have arisen in connection with the method to be explained hereafter. These are superior to the "heat" and other stages of the śrāvakas and others;

their roots of merit, such as "heat," have as their object the four truths characterized by entities such as form (rūpaṇa) and so forth, which are established in the aspects of impermanence and so on as an antidote to the view of self, and serve as the cause for the realization of one's own vehicle.
Because it is established that the fourfold conceptualization is non-associated [with the true nature],
the aids to penetration for Bodhisattvas— by the power of skillful means— are sometimes by way of the cause and sometimes by way of the fruit.

It should be understood that the objective support of the four truths consists of the entities [of suffering and so forth], sometimes by way of their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and sometimes by way of their characteristic (*dharmatākāra*), according to one’s spiritual capacity (*yathābhavyatā*).
This has not been elaborated upon, as the intention was merely to provide a concise explanation.
Since this is the established position, one should not raise any objection whatsoever by resorting to another vehicle.
To the question, "What is the distinction between the object (*ālambana*) and the aspect (*ākāra*)?", he states the object and the aspect through seven intermediate verses:
"The object consists of impermanence and so forth, based upon the [four] truths; its aspect is the mental image thereof."
The negation of attachment and so forth is the cause for attaining the three vehicles.
The arising and passing away of form and so forth, as well as their dispersion and persistence, are designated as being inexpressible.
In that regard, for the beginner, the object of focus consists of the sixteen aspects such as impermanence, which are based upon the four truths beginning with suffering.
The negation of the focal objects and so forth that involve adherence to the truths of suffering and the rest constitutes its formal aspect.
It should be understood that all [stages] beginning with "Heat" (ūṣmagata) serve as the causal basis for attaining the realization of the three vehicles.

Because one practices the negation and non-apprehension of form and so forth respectively through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and mental attention to reality (*tattvamanasikāra*), there is no perception [of them]; this is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the middle [stage].
Because all designations are absent, there is the absence of both the characteristics of a dissimilar continuity and a similar continuity; this is the aspect (*ākṛti*).
From form up to the Buddha, all phenomena are conventional and worldly; this is the object of the superior [level].
The nature of phenomena, such as the wholesome and so forth, cannot be expressed by anyone; this is its aspect.
Because it possesses both an object and an aspect and serves as the precursor to the fire of non-conceptual knowledge, "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) is of three kinds.
Their abiding in form and so forth is, by virtue of that [abiding], their lack of intrinsic nature.
The mutual nature of those two is the non-establishment of their impermanence and so forth;
the emptiness of those [characteristics] of that [nature] is the mutual naturelessness of these two.
Non-apprehension of phenomena is the non-contemplation of their signs;
it is the investigation by means of wisdom through the non-perception of everything. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.31)
Thus: here, by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), form and the other aggregates are devoid of an intrinsic nature by way of their own nature as form and so forth;
therefore, "the non-abiding of form and the rest" is the object (*ālambana*) for the weak [level of practice].

Since, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), form and all other phenomena and emptiness are mutually one and the same form, there is an absence of impermanence and so forth within emptiness; thus, the mental aspect (*ākāra*) is that there is no abiding in form and the rest by way of permanence, impermanence, and so forth.

Because the emptinesses of impermanence and so forth lack intrinsic nature by virtue of being the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, there is a mutual identity among these emptinesses; this is the object of the medium [level of practice].
That which is the non-appropriation of form and so forth through the negation of intrinsic nature is the aspect (*ākāra*).
Because form and so forth do not perceive signs such as blue precisely due to the absence of intrinsic nature, this is the object of the superior [level of practice].

The aspect [of this stage] is the investigation of all things through wisdom by means of the correct discernment of phenomena (*samyag-dharmapravicaya*), characterized by their non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*). Thus, because it possesses both an object and an aspect, and because it represents the summit of the unstable roots of merit, it is called "the Summit" (*mūrdhan*); it is of three kinds.
The absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*) in form and so forth is the very nature of that absence.
That is non-arising, non-emergence, purity, and signlessness.
"Non-adherence to those signs, non-conviction, and the state of non-perception.

Herein, emptiness is the object of focus for the beginner (*mṛdu*), consisting in the lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) of form and so forth due to the oneness of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Its mental aspect (*ākāra*) is that form and so forth have the nature of non-existence with respect to the person who perceives them.
The object of focus for the middling [level] is the non-arising and non-cessation of form and so forth by virtue of their being devoid of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtyasvabhāvatva*).

The aspect is the purification of the body and so forth in all their modes through the realization of the true nature of all phenomena. The object of focus for the superior [level] is the signlessness (*animittatva*) of all phenomena due to the non-occurrence of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

The aspect [of this stage] is the non-comprehension of the mental application of conviction and the mental application of reality-as-it-is, because by their very nature the signs of form and so forth lack a basis for conviction.

Thus, because one endures the superior Dharma through the absence of rebirth in the lower realms, being endowed with both the object and the aspect, there are three types of the stage of Patience (kṣānti).
[Verse 1.33: Samādhi is its activity; prediction is the exhaustion of mentation.

The mutual intrinsic nature of the triad and the non-conceptuality of meditative concentration—this constitutes the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) according to their degrees of weak, medium, and intense. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 1.34.

Thus: here, the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on the non-arising of all phenomena and on the "heroic strides" (*vīraṅgama*) and so forth is to be cultivated; this is the object of focus (*ālambana*) for the weak [level].

The mode of activity (*ākāra*) is that the operation of the concentration proceeds effortlessly in all world-systems according to the capacity of beings, by the power of one's own vows, merit, wisdom, and the *dharmadhātu*.

This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): that a yogin who has correctly entered into concentration is granted a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) by the Buddhas; this is the object of focus for the middling [level].

The aspect is that for a bodhisattva who has realized the true nature of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through the non-arising of all conceptual constructions, cognitions such as "I am absorbed" do not occur.

The object of focus for the superior [level] is that, by way of the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*), these three—the absorption, the bodhisattva, and the meaning of the perfection of wisdom—are mutually one and the same form.
The aspect is that the non-conceptualization of absorption, due to the non-existence of all phenomena, is the supreme skillful means.

Thus, there are three types called the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*agradharma*), so named because they are the foremost of all mundane phenomena by virtue of their objects (*ālambana*) and aspects (*ākāra*). Regarding the object—such as impermanence and so forth—which is based upon the [four] truths: even though one may speak of the "dharma" and the "possessor of the dharma" (*dharmī*) when referring to the object and the distinguished aspect, in every case where one speaks of the "dharma" that distinguishes the object, there is no exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions.
This is because of the principle that there is no distinction whatsoever between these two.

Alternatively, in accordance with the meter of the verse (*kārikā*), although they are expressed differently, since both involve the negation of adherence (*abhiniveśa*) and so forth, and are in reality devoid of affirmation and negation, the object (*ālambana*) and the aspect (*ākāra*) are treated as being included within the truths of suffering and the rest.
The same should be understood in other instances as well.
To clarify the meaning of the combination of the four types of conceptualization, he states two intermediate verses:
"The duality of the conceptualization of the apprehended object arises from [the perception of] the thing itself and its counteragent."
Furthermore, through the divisions of the mass of delusion and so forth, each of these is ninefold.
Thus, based on the two modes—namely, as the basis for defiled things and as the basis for their antidotes—the divisions of ignorance and the aggregates of purification are ninefold.
The grasper is considered to be twofold, based on substantiality and designation:
[the former] in the form of an independent self and so forth, and [the latter] by relying upon the aggregates and so forth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.36)

Thus it is said. Here, there are two kinds of conceptualization of the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*), namely: [the conceptualization of] a person as substantially existent (*dravyasat*) and [the conceptualization of] a person as nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*). Each of these is further divided into nine types based on the apprehension of a self, the aggregates (*skandha*), and so forth, as independent entities.
In this regard, the summary of the meaning is as follows: they have the basis of the objects of affliction (*saṃkleśavastu*)... [as follows].

The conceptualizations of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*) consist of: attachment to ignorance, the aggregates such as form, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the two extremes; ignorance regarding affliction and purification; non-abiding on the noble path; apprehension; and the conceptualization of the self and so forth as being pure, arising, and so on.

Furthermore, the conceptualizations of the apprehended consist of the antidotes, the bases, the accumulations, the gateways, the lineages, arising, emptiness, the meaning of the perfections (*pāramitā*), seeing and meditating, and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

The conceptualizations of the apprehender (*grāhaka-vikalpa*) consist of those based on a person (*pudgala*) as a real substance: namely, the independent self, the single cause, the self as a seer and so forth, the self as affliction, detachment, seeing and meditating, and the basis for one who has accomplished his purpose.

The conceptualizations of the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*) have as their basis persons existing as designations (*prajñaptisat*), namely: the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense-fields (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), purification (*vyavadāna*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Thus, these four types of conceptualization are respectively associated with the four levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Although the "comprehensive grasp" (*samparigraha*) was previously mentioned in accordance with the *Sambaddhakārikā*, the following intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*) is stated immediately after that to demonstrate that by its power, the aforementioned distinctions arise.

The non-depression of the mind and so forth, the teaching on the lack of intrinsic nature and so forth, the abandonment of their opposites, and the complete embrace [of the path]—these constitute [the perfection of wisdom]. (Abhis 1.37)

Through skill in means—such as not being discouraged by the weakness of the mind and being free from fear—one who, according to the inclinations [of others], is free from opposing factors such as stinginess and teaches the selflessness of all things and so forth, is a "spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*); this constitutes "thoroughly embracing" (4). Regarding the basis of practice, he explains the basis of practice for one who possesses practice, which consists of the aforementioned aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), as well as other stages such as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth: [The verse: The basis of practice is said to be the spiritual friend, Who, through skill in means, does not become weary, And who, according to the inclinations [of others], Teaches the selflessness of all things and so forth. [The commentary: By means of skill in means—characterized by not being discouraged and not being terrified—one who is free from opposing factors such as stinginess, and who teaches the selflessness of all things and so forth in accordance with the inclinations [of others], is a "spiritual friend. This is "thorough embracing. (4) He states the basis of practice for the practitioner, which consists of the aforementioned aids to penetration, as well as other stages such as the path of seeing and so forth. Thus, he speaks of the basis of practice.
Of the dharma of the sixfold realization, of the abandonment of the opposites, of the full utilization of those two, and of wisdom together with compassion. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.38)

The lineage (gotra) is said to be the foundation for the uniqueness of the disciple, the sequence of activity for the sake of others, and the effortless operation of primordial wisdom. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.39)

In this regard, first of all, there is the basis for the arising of the fourfold mundane aids to penetration (*laukikanirvedhabhāgīya*); then, that of the supramundane paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
and subsequently, by the power of their arising, the simultaneous production of all antidotes and the cessation of all discordant factors, like the expulsion of thieves and the closing of a door.
Then, through the non-perception of that [duality], there is the departure from conceptual constructions associated with the arising and ceasing of that [duality].
Thereafter, by the power of previous vows and skillful means such as generosity, there is the non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through wisdom and compassion.
Finally, through the arising of those, there is the quality that is not shared with the śrāvakas and others.

Then, there is the sequence of the benefit for others, characterized by the establishment of [beings] in the three vehicles through the gateway of intentions such as introducing them according to their dispositions;
and then, the basis for the non-conceptual, effortless knowledge that benefits others as long as saṃsāra lasts.
This is precisely the sequence.
By this alone, all human goals are accomplished.

It has been taught that the lineage (*gotra*) is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*, which serves as the support for the aforementioned qualities and consists of thirteen types of Bodhisattvas distinguished by differences in their stages of the dharma of practice.

If it is because the *dharmadhātu* itself is the cause for the realization of the noble qualities that the Bodhisattva—whose essence is that [dharmadhātu]—is the naturally abiding lineage of the unsurpassed Buddha-qualities;

At that time, fearing that a person of dull intellect might suspect that [the lineage] does not belong to the Bodhisattva alone because it exists as a universal [characteristic], he speaks this intermediate verse:

"Because the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is undifferentiated, a distinction of lineages (*gotra*) is not tenable. This is also a resolution: although one may apprehend [the path] according to the sequence of realization in the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth, it is designated as a "lineage" because the realm of phenomena is established as the causal basis for the realization of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*).
Nevertheless, for the sake of ease, he states another summary by means of a worldly analogy:
"But its differentiation is proclaimed due to the differentiation of the qualities to be contained within it. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.40)

Just as there is a distinction among vessels—such as jars—which are produced from the same clay substance and baked by the same fire, based on their function as containers for different contents like honey or sugar; in the same way, the multiplicity of the receptacles is taught through the multiplicity of the dharmas to be realized and contained within them, which are subsumed under the three vehicles.
5. The Object of Cognition (*ālambana*).
Regarding the question of what the objective support (*ālambana*) is for the basis of the practice as described, he says:

"The objective support consists of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); these, moreover, are the wholesome and so forth, those known as mundane attainments, and those considered supramundane. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.41)
Dharmas with outflows and without outflows, those which are conditioned and unconditioned,
those dharmas shared with disciples, and those that are unique to the Sage.

In that regard, first of all, generally speaking, [all phenomena] (*sarvadharmāḥ*) are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, respectively: such as the state of being a recluse (*śrāmaṇyatā*), killing, and so forth, or neutral bodily actions and so on.
Then, for those very same [phenomena], there are four remaining divisions, categorized as mundane (*laukika*) and so forth.
Respectively, these are: the five aggregates associated with ordinary worldlings;
the four meditative absorptions comprised by all noble beings;
and the five aggregates of clinging, which do not serve as an antidote to the view of self.
The four foundations of mindfulness serve as the antidote to that [view].
The realms of desire and so forth are dependent upon causes and conditions;
suchness is independent of causes.
The four dhyānas arise from the mental continuums of all noble beings;

the ten powers possess the nature of arising from the continuum of a perfectly enlightened Buddha. Thus, by means of this sequence of realization, all phenomena are apprehended as they truly are; this is the elevenfold object of focus (*ālambana*).
6. Summary.
Regarding the question of what the objective of such a realization of the focal object is, he states the objective:

"The objective of the Self-Existent Ones should be understood as consisting in the three greatnesses within the triad of supremacy over all beings, the abandonment of the mind, and attainment. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.43)

In every respect, through the thorough knowledge of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because one has set out in practice with reference to the greatness of mind— the preeminence over the entire mass of beings and the entire community of beings— of future Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the greatness of abandonment and the greatness of realization, and because it possesses these three kinds of greatness, the objective (*samuddeśa*) is threefold.
It is to be known.
7. Having thus explained the basis of practice and so forth—namely, the practice of armor—if one asks, "Furthermore, what is its essential nature? [the following is stated].
That practice, characterized by the realization [of the path], has as its basis the white dharmas in general within the domain of the three types of omniscience,

and as its basis the six perfections in each respective clear realization (*pratyabhisamaya*) throughout the fourfold clear realizations beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).

Thus, among the [four]— armor, setting out, equipment, and departure— which are the nature of the paths of application, seeing, cultivation, and the special [path], and which are characterized by practice, [this is the practice].
Regarding the first practice, that of armor, he speaks of it by way of its nature as vigor:

"The practice of armor is that which consists in the collective inclusion of each of those sixfold [perfections] within giving and the others; it is described as being composed of six groups of six. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.44)
Thus: in the giving of the gift of Dharma and other gifts, there is the avoidance of mental orientations such as those of the Śrāvakas; patience toward speaking unpleasant words to all people;
and the generation of aspiration.

The undistracted one-pointedness unmixed with other vehicles and the dedication toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment are respectively performed by means of the armor of the non-apprehension of the gift and so forth;
in the very same way, there is the guarding of ethical discipline and the accomplishment of patience.
The undertaking of vigor, the accomplishment of meditative concentration,

and the cultivation of wisdom— in this way, when each of the six perfections beginning with generosity is subsumed within generosity and the others, there are thirty-six branches by means of six sets of six; and because they share the common characteristics of generosity and the rest, they are also categorized as six.
The practices of armor arise.
8. Regarding the practice of setting out (*prasthāna-pratipatti*):
since one who has donned the armor proceeds in this manner, he speaks of the second [practice], the practice of setting out.

In the meditative absorptions and formless attainments, in generosity and the rest, in the paths, in loving-kindness and the like, in the application of the perception of an object, and in the purifications of the three spheres; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.45.

In the summary, in the six superknowledges, and in the method of the knowledge of all aspects, the setting out and the practice are to be known for those who ascend the Great Vehicle. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.46)

The practice of setting out (*prasthāna-pratipatti*) is ninefold, characterized by correct establishment in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the six perfections beginning with generosity (*dāna*), the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the special path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-viśeṣa-mārga*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*), the purification of all things as the three spheres (*sarva-vastu-trimaṇḍala-viśuddhi*), the summary topics (*uddeśa*), the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); its nature is the traversing of all Mahāyāna dharmas.
9. The practice of equipment (*sambhāra-pratipatti*).
Having thus described the setting forth, he states the third practice, the practice of the equipment (sambhāra-pratipatti):
"Compassion, the sixfold group beginning with giving, calm abiding together with insight, the path that is yoked in union, and skill in means. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.47)
Knowledge, merit, the path, the dhāraṇīs, and the ten stages; as well as the counteragent—these are to be known as the sequence of the practice of the accumulations. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.48)

Because one practices the entire meaning of the Mahāyāna by means of these— compassion and so forth— through the non-apprehension of great compassion, generosity, ethical discipline, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, the path of the union of calm abiding and insight, skill in means, primordial wisdom, merit, the path beginning with vision, the dhāraṇīs beginning with speech, the stages, and the remedies, yet without transcending conventional truth;

and because they possess the nature of correct practice and encompass great enlightenment, there are seventeen practices of the accumulations, known as the "accumulations of great compassion and so forth."

In that regard, the equipment of wisdom (*jñāna-sambhāra*) is twentyfold, distinguished by the various types of emptiness: internal, external, both internal and external, great, ultimate, conditioned, unconditioned, past, infinite, beginningless and endless, non-dispersal, essential nature, the non-apprehension of the characteristics of all phenomena, the absence of intrinsic nature, the existence of the absence of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of other-nature.

[The emptiness of] the internal, the external, and both; likewise, [the emptiness of] the directions, of nirvāṇa, and of the meaning; and [the emptiness] of the conditioned and the unconditioned. // 1 //

Because it is absolutely without end or beginning, because it is unconditioned and uncreated, and furthermore, because it possesses the characteristic of being all phenomena and because it transcends past, present, and future. // 2 //
Due to their being produced by conjunction, their being entities, and their having the nature of space and emptiness;
and because they are devoid of their own intrinsic nature, twenty types of emptiness are recognized. (3)
In order to demonstrate the dharmas that are being perfected through the equipment for the stages (*bhūmisambhāra*) as they pertain to the ten stages, twenty-three intermediate verses are spoken:
1. The first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), is attained through ten kinds of preparatory cultivation (*parikarman*).
The intention consists in the state of being a beneficial thing and equanimity of mind toward sentient beings. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.49)
Renunciation, service to friends, seeking the foundation of the true Dharma, constant state of mind directed toward renunciation, and longing for the body of a Buddha. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.50)

The teaching of the Dharma is intended as the tenth statement, which is truth; and their cultivation is to be understood through the non-apprehension of their intrinsic nature. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.51)
Thus: an intention free from crookedness toward all things as they truly are,
being beneficial in one's own and others' purposes,
and equanimity of mind toward all sentient beings.
The relinquishment of all possessions,
the propitiation of spiritual friends,
and the pursuit of the objects of the sublime Dharma as comprised within the three vehicles.
Disinterest in dwelling in a household,
longing for the unsurpassed body of a Buddha,
and the proclamation of the true Dharma.
Because it arises in every way through these ten characteristic qualities— truthfulness and so forth—

which serve as purifications and specific causes, and because its intrinsic nature is non-apprehendable through the very purification of its specific characteristics, the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), is attained.
2. The second stage is Vimalā (The Stainless).

It consists of ethical discipline, gratitude, patience, great joy, vast compassion, reverence, service to the teachers, and eighthly, vigor in giving and the other perfections. Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.52.

Thus are the ethical discipline of the performance of beneficial actions for sentient beings and the ethical discipline of restraint; the non-forgetfulness (non-ruination) of benefits conferred by others;
and patience toward harms and the like inflicted by others.
Freedom from regret in the accomplishment of wholesome qualities,
loving-kindness toward all people,
and prostration before preceptors and others.

The second stage, the *Vimalā* (Stainless), is attained through these eight kinds of factors characterized by the specific preparations consisting of the practice of the Dharma taught by spiritual friends and the pursuit of the six perfections, such as generosity.
3. The *Prabhākarī* (Luminous) Stage.
Insatiability regarding learning, giving that is free from worldly motives, the complete purification of the Buddha-field, and lack of weariness with cyclic existence; Abhis 1.53.
"Shame and dread of blame— these five are of the nature of reflection.
This refers to the lack of satiety in hearing the true Dharma and the proclamation of the true Dharma with a mind free from regard for gain and other such things.

The third stage, the Prabhākarī (Luminous), is realized through fivefold preparation—just as before—consisting of: the purification of one's own buddha-field, both its basis and its supported contents; the absence of weariness by seeing that one has benefited sentient beings despite their contrary behavior; and the non-performance of unwholesome dharmas with regard to oneself and others; and finally, the preparation regarding the realization of the nature of things as previously understood.
4. The Radiant Stage (*arciṣmatī bhūmiḥ*):
freedom from desire for worldly gain, having few wishes, contentment, and the practice of the ascetic purifications and austerities.
Not abandoning the training, revulsion toward sensual desires, world-weariness, the relinquishing of all things, being undaunted, and being free from expectation; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.55.
Thus: dwelling in the forest,
lack of longing for gains not yet obtained,
and absence of excessive solicitation for gains already obtained.
The concealment of virtues purified by alms-seeking and other practices;
the non-abandonment of even life and limb for those who have undertaken the training;
and the censure of the qualities of sensual desire through the perception of their faults.
Inclination toward nirvana in accordance with those to be trained,
the relinquishment of all possessions,
and an absence of mental contraction in the accomplishment of wholesome deeds.
The fourth stage, Arciṣmatī, is ascended in ten ways as previously described, beginning with "disregard for all things.
The fifth stage, Sudurjayā,
[is characterized by] avoiding intimacy, family possessiveness, and places that lead to social distraction.
Self-exaltation and contempt for others, and the ten unwholesome paths of action.
By abandoning pride, arrogance, error, doubt, and the endurance of afflictions, one attains these ten [qualities] on the fifth stage.
Thus: dwelling together with householders, renunciants, and others for the sake of gain and so forth;
showing oneself to families that are faithful;
and [residing in] cities and other places crowded with people.
Self-praise and disparaging others,
the ten paths of unwholesome action,
and conceit regarding learning and so forth.
Not bowing down to others,
adherence to what is wholesome, unwholesome, or perverted,
and wrong views and other forms of faulty intellect.

By abandoning these ten factors characterized as such— namely, the manifestation of all afflictions such as passion and so forth— one proceeds, by means of the tenfold preparatory cultivation (parikarma) consisting of the opposite qualities implied by their negation,
as previously described, to ascend to the fifth stage, the *Sudurjayā* (The Very Difficult to Conquer).
This is the sixth [stage], the *Abhimukhī* (The Manifest).

Through the complete fulfillment of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, he avoids those whose minds are characterized by longing for discipleship, the desire for the rhinoceros-like [solitary] state, or fear. // Abhis 1.58 //
Being asked, he is not discouraged; even when giving away everything, his mind is not troubled;
though emaciated, he does not reject those who seek his help—he attains the sixth stage. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.59)

By fulfilling the six perfections beginning with generosity; by abandoning the longing for the state of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha; by abandoning fear regarding the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature; by abandoning shrinking back when requested by beggars; by abandoning dejection when giving away all one's possessions spontaneously; and by abandoning a mind that rejects supplicants due to poverty—thus, through these twelve purificatory practices as previously described, the sixth stage, the Abhimukhī, is realized.
7. The Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṅgamā bhūmi*):

[It is characterized by] the grasping at a self and a sentient being, the views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding the living being and the person, and [the grasping at] signs, causes, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.60)
Establishment in the three realms, attachment, and a mind that is cowed; as well as adherence to views regarding the Three Jewels and the precepts. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.61)
He for whom the twenty stains— consisting of disputes regarding emptiness and opposition to it—
are severed, reaches the seventh stage.

Thus, by the removal of these twenty kinds of stains—namely, [the views of] self, sentient being, life-force, person, annihilationism, eternalism, signs, causes, and the bases of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields within the three realms; as well as the attachment and clinging of a mind that is fixated and submerged [in objects]; and the grasping and rejection arising from disputes and contradictions regarding emptiness, the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, morality, and views—one attains the seventh stage, the "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṅgamā*), through the twentyfold preparatory dharmas that counteract those erroneous states, as previously described.
To provide an exposition of the nature of reality (dharmatā) as implied by the meaning [of the preceding], he says:

Knowledge of the three gates of liberation, the purity of the three spheres, compassion, non-conceptualization, and the knowledge of the single principle of the equality of all phenomena. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.63)

The knowledge of receptivity to non-arising, the unified comprehension of all phenomena, the uprooting of conceptual construction, and the abandonment of perceptions, views, and afflictions. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.64)
The stabilization of calm abiding, skill in insight, the taming of the mind, and knowledge that is unimpeded everywhere. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.65)
The absence of attachment, moving at will to other fields simultaneously, and the perception of one's own self-nature everywhere—these constitute the twenty [qualities]. (Abhis 1.66)
It is the correct knowledge of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the non-apprehension of the killer, the slain, and the killing within the ten paths of wholesome action;
and compassion directed toward all sentient beings as its object.
The non-apprehension of objects, the awakening to the equality of all phenomena,
and the awakening to the single vehicle of the Mahāyāna.
Thorough knowledge of non-arising, realization through the patient acceptance of profound reflection on the Dharma,
and the illumination of all objects of knowledge by means of the gateway of Mahāyāna skillful methods.
The severance of all conceptual constructions;

the absence of the conceptualization that grasps at signs; the relinquishing of the five views, such as the view of a self-existent body; and the avoidance of the afflictions, such as attachment and so forth.
The cultivation of calm abiding,
skill in wisdom,
and the pacification of the mind.
Knowledge of the non-obstruction by form and so forth,
the absence of any basis for dogmatic attachment,
and the ability to travel to buddha-fields at will and simultaneously.
The manifestation of one's own body everywhere in accordance with those to be trained—by means of these twenty modes of preparatory dharma as before, the seventh bhūmi is attained.
8. The Immovable Bhūmi (Acalā):
the knowledge of the minds of all sentient beings, the play of the supernormal powers, and the auspicious.
The perfection of the buddha-field occurs through the service and examination of the Buddhas.
Sensory cognition, the purification of the Buddha-field, abiding like an illusion, and the intentional assumption of existence—this eightfold activity has been taught. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.68)
Thus: the knowledge of the mental activities of all sentient beings as they truly are;
sporting with the supernormal powers (*ṛddhyabhijñā*) within the world-system; and the transformation of the supporting buddha-field into the nature of gold and other precious substances.
The honoring of the Buddhas through the examination of all aspects of phenomena,
the accomplishment of the divine eye,
and the purification of the buddha-field and its sentient beings to be supported.

Abiding everywhere in the state of being like an illusion, and taking birth intentionally for the sake of seeing the welfare of all sentient beings—through the cultivation of these eight kinds of qualities as before, the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), is experienced. 9. The Stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī).
The infinite aspirations, the knowledge of the languages of gods and others, eloquence like a flowing river, and the supreme descent into the womb—[these are the marks]. Abhis 1.69.
And regarding noble birth, lineage, clan, retinue, and birth;
concerning renunciation, the tree of enlightenment, the abundance of qualities, and one's own perfections—[these are the ten powers]. Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.70.
Thus: infinite aspiration,
knowledge of the sounds of all sentient beings such as gods,
and inexhaustible eloquence comparable to a river.
The descent into the womb praised by all people,
the status of being a king and so forth, and lineage from the sun and other [divinities].
One who possesses kinsmen well-connected through their mothers and others,
whose retinue is under one's own command,
and whose birth is celebrated by Śakra and the other gods;

The ninth stage, Sādhumatī, is characterized by twelve preparations consisting of perfections (*sampatti-lakṣaṇa*), as previously performed with specific preparations: the departure through the exhortation of the Buddhas and others; the Aśvattha tree resembling a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*); and the fulfillment of the qualities of the nature of the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma.
The stage is directly realized.

Having thus explained the preparatory practices for the tenth stage, Dharmameghā, by way of its being the causal stage, [the author] does not describe those [practices] separately as the resultant stage, but rather states the characteristics of the tenth stage by means of a summary:

10. The Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi). Having thus pointed out the preparatory practices for that [stage] by way of its being a causal stage, he states the definition of the tenth stage by way of its being a resultant stage, without mentioning them individually, through a summary:
Having transcended the nine stages, one is established in the stage of a Buddha;
that by which this is known is to be understood as the tenth bodhisattva stage. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.71)

Thus, with the intention of establishing three systems for the six [categories]— namely, those belonging to the lineages of the śrāvakas and so forth, those entering the first fruit, stream-enterers (srotāpanna), once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returners (anāgāmin), and arhats— the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are, respectively: the lineage stage (gotrabhūmi), the eighth stage (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi), the seeing stage (darśana-bhūmi), the refinement stage (tanu-bhūmi), the stage of one who has become free from passion (vītarāga-bhūmi), the stage of one who has completed the task (kṛtavi-bhūmi), and the stage of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha (which subsumes the remaining three types of enterers).

Since it is stated that "having thus transcended the nine stages consisting of the ninefold [path] as described for bodhisattvas, on the tenth stage, a bodhisattva is to be called a Buddha, but not a *samyaksaṃbuddha*," one should understand that the very tenth bodhisattva stage is that which consists in the wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-jñāna*) by which one abides on the Buddha-stage.
(The Accumulation of Counteragents) To explain the accumulation of counteragents, he states an intermediate verse:
"The counteragent is to be known as eightfold on the paths of seeing and cultivation."
For the pacification of the eight conceptual constructions of the grasped and the grasper.

Thus, because the two types of conceptualization regarding the object— namely, the conceptualization of the apprehended based on the mere defiled entities and the conceptualization of the apprehended based on the person as a substantial entity or a designated entity— and the two types of conceptualization regarding the subject— namely, the conceptualization of the apprehender based on the person as a substantial entity or a designated entity— are abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, there are eight types of antidotes to be realized by relying upon the two truths during the very stages of the two paths, according to the distinction of the factors to be countered, for the sake of pacifying the eight conceptualizations of apprehended and apprehender.
10. The practice of departure (*niryāṇapratipatti*): He explains the fourth [practice], the practice of departure, as "departure for one who has thus accumulated the provisions":
regarding the objective, regarding equanimity, regarding the welfare of sentient beings, and regarding the absence of effort.
And there is the departure for the ultimate, which is the departure characterized by attainment.
And the departure into the knowledge of all aspects is the domain of the path;
this eightfold nature is to be known as the practice of departure. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.74)
Thus: the aforementioned summary,
the equality of all phenomena, and the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings.
It is effortless because it performs all activities without signs; it is a specific state free from eternalism and nihilism;
and it is the attainment of all goals of the three vehicles.

The practice of departure (*niryāṇapratipatti*) is eightfold, consisting of these eight aspects: because there is no other distinct dharma among the objects of departure—such as the aforementioned omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the path distinguished by it—all things are non-apprehendable. Thus ends the commentary on the first chapter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom.
The Second Chapter: Knowledge of the Path (Mārgajñatā).

1—Since the realization of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot occur without a thorough understanding of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*), he explains the knowledge of the path:
