The signs of the afflictions and their characteristics, the discordant factors and their remedies, solitude, the difficult-to-practice solitary state, and the objective that is non-apprehension; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.29.

That which is attachment to the prohibited, that which is designated as an objective support, that which is misconception, and that which is non-obstructive—these are without basis, without coming, and without birth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.30)
The non-apprehension of suchness and its sixteenfold nature, as well as the fact that it is perceived like a characteristic—this is considered the fourth characteristic. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.31)

Thus: the fourfold nature of discernment regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) by way of the emptiness of (1) the afflictions such as attachment and their concomitants, (2) the physical dysfunctions (*kāyadauṣṭhulya*) that are their signs, (3) the improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) caused by them, and (4) the objects of attachment and non-attachment along with their respective antidotes; and the negation of adherence to all entities, characterized by (5) the non-perception of the phenomena of the object and subject of meditation—namely, the ultimate non-existence of sentient beings, parinirvāṇa, the performer of difficult deeds, the one-sidedness of falling into other vehicles, and the supreme goal to be accomplished over a long period—these are the five natures of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
It has as its object the specific categories subsumed under the knowledge of the path to omniscience;
it is characterized by non-delusion because it teaches in a manner that does not contradict worldly understanding and conventions;
and it is the knowledge that does not obstruct form and the other sense objects.
It is non-abiding through the non-apprehension of knowledge and the object of knowledge;
it is non-coming through suchness;
it is unborn through the lack of intrinsic nature in form and the other aggregates.
"The non-apprehension of the three natures, such as existence, non-existence, and so forth"—these are the seven natures of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Thus, by means of these sixteen natures, the applications to the three types of omniscience are characterized as it truly is; this is considered the fourth characteristic, the characteristic of nature (*svabhāvalakṣaṇa*).
In this way, when taken together in one place, there are ninety-one characteristics in total.
6. Regarding the "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*):

since the thorough knowledge of the aforementioned application occurs only for one who possesses the roots of merit conducive to liberation, he speaks of that which is conducive to liberation as "skill in the accomplishment of signless giving and so forth."
In this realization of all aspects, that which is conducive to liberation is intended.

Thus [it is said]. In this realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), skillfulness alone regarding the full attainment within one's own continuum—beginning with the perfections such as giving and ending with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—is characterized by the mode of knowledge that takes the signless (*animitta*) as its object.
Furthermore, to demonstrate what that skillfulness is, he states two intermediate verses:
"Faith has the Buddha and so forth as its object; vigor has the sphere of giving and so forth as its object."
Mindfulness is the perfection of intention; meditative concentration is non-conceptuality. // Abhis 4.33 //
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the knowledge of all phenomena in all their aspects; it is fivefold.
Complete awakening (*sambodhi*) is considered easy to realize through sharp [faculties], but difficult to realize through dull ones. (Abhis 4.34)

Thus, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and distinguished wisdom—which do not have the nature of sense faculties—are skillfulness regarding five kinds of objects, respectively: [the Buddha], the perfection of the intention for giving, non-conceptuality, and the thorough knowledge of all phenomena in all their aspects. Even so, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not attained by everyone.
This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): since perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is easily realized through superior degrees of faith and the other [faculties],
while it is difficult to realize through those same faculties when they are weak— this being the implied meaning—
it follows that the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha* is attained through middling degrees, and the enlightenment of a *śrāvaka* through weak degrees.
7. Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*):
since the aids to penetration arise for one who has already produced the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and is diligent, it is said:
"In this context, all sentient beings are taught as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the 'heat' (*ūṣman*) stage."
The ten aspects, beginning with equanimity of mind, are taught as being directed toward those very same objects. // Abhis 4.35 //

For one who has personally desisted from evil and is established in giving and other virtues, there is the enjoining of others to those two, as well as conformity through speaking their praise. (Abhis 4.36)

The Summits, the Patience, and likewise the Supreme Mundane Dharmas are to be understood through [the practices of] maturing sentient beings and so forth, which have themselves and others as their basis and consist of the knowledge of reality. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.37)

Thus, in this *sarvākārābhisambodhi*, the stage of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) is intended with respect to sentient beings as its object through five aspects of mind—equanimity, loving-kindness, benefit, non-resistance, and non-harming—and through another five aspects of mind: the mind [of one toward] a mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister, kinsman, and blood relative.
In brief, it consists of the abandonment and adoption, respectively, of the unwholesome and the wholesome, by one who has personally desisted from the former and engaged in the latter.

Through that [means], there are two aspects: turning others away from evil and engaging them in the wholesome. Likewise, when others engage [in the wholesome] spontaneously, there are two aspects: praising [their action] and being compliant. Thus, through this twofold classification of the Dharma, the aspects are infinite; in this way, one reaches the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) stage with respect to the objective support of sentient beings.
Just as in the case of the Summits, the objective supports and aspects are distinguished by the differentiation between oneself and others.

Likewise, through aspects such as application, praise, and conformity, there is the very objectification (*ālambana*) of the truths of suffering and so forth based on oneself and others; this constitutes *kṣānti*.

As before, through aspects such as maturing and liberating oneself and others, there are the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) which have sentient beings as their object; thus they constitute the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

By means of the differentiation of the cultivation of the objects of the path in all their aspects, there occurs, in due order within the three types of clear realization beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the attainment of the supramundane paths of seeing and meditation, preceded by the attainment of the mundane aids to penetration.

However, it should be understood that regarding the threefold clear realization beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), undefiled knowledge— comprised of the path distinguished by all aspects— is produced through the gradual sequence of weak, medium, and intense stages according to the successive distinctions of cultivation; thus, the designations such as "aids to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are stated in order to refute the notion of simultaneous production.
8. The Irreversible Assembly:

Regarding the assembly of irreversible bodhisattvas, [the author] states the characteristics of the irreversible bodhisattva assembly by explaining that the aforementioned aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) arise [for them]:
"Based upon the factors of penetration, [they exist] in the paths of seeing and cultivation."
Those bodhisattvas who abide [in this] constitute here the irreversible group.

Thus: those heroes who abide in the four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) by way of the respective realizations of the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) which will be explained hereafter—they alone constitute the irreversible community of bodhisattvas in training (*śaikṣa*).

Furthermore, if one asks what their unique characteristics (*āveṇikalakṣaṇa*) are, [the author] first states the characteristics of those abiding in the aids to penetration with a single intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*):

Through these twenty signs, such as the turning away from form and so forth, which have been established, this is the characteristic of the non-retrogressive state for one who abides in the factors of penetration. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 4.39.

Thus, the characteristic of non-retrogression for those abiding in the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) should be understood through twenty modes, such as the cessation of form and so forth, and freedom from doubt.
If one asks what the characteristics of cessation and the others are, [the author] says the following in order to demonstrate them with six intermediate verses:
"Cessation of form and so forth, freedom from doubt, and the destruction of moments..."
Establishing oneself in what is wholesome and then enjoining others to do the same.
Generosity and the rest are dependent on others; lack of desire even for profound meanings;
friendliness; non-dwelling with body and so forth; and [the absence of] the fivefold obscuration. (Abhis 4.41)
The abandonment of all latent tendencies, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and purity; the robes and other requisites [are pure], and there is no arising of worms within the body. // Abhis 4.42 //

Absence of crookedness in thought, undertaking of ascetic practices, freedom from envy and the like, proceeding in accordance with the nature of reality, and seeking even the hells for the sake of the world. (Abhis 4.43)

Not being led astray by others, recognizing as Māra himself anyone who teaches another path, and awakening to the very fact that he is Māra—this is the conduct approved by the Buddhas. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.44)
Established in the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
one does not turn back from perfect enlightenment by virtue of these twenty signs.
Thus: because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*), there is a turning away from phenomena such as form (*rūpa*);
through the attainment of serene confidence (*avetyaprasāda*), there is the destruction of doubt;

and through the fulfillment of one's vow (*praṇidhāna*), there is the destruction of the eight inopportune births (*akṣaṇa*): namely, false views, rebirth in the hells, as a hungry ghost (*preta*), or an animal, not hearing the Buddha’s word, birth in a border region, being deficient in faculties, being dull-witted or mute, and rebirth among long-lived gods.

Through compassion, it is the application of oneself and others to the qualities of virtue; through the exchange of self and others, it is giving and so forth dedicated toward the welfare of other sentient beings;
and through the correct awakening to the Dharma, it is the longing for the meaning of the profound Dharma.

Through being engaged in the welfare of others, there is the action of body, speech, and mind characterized by loving-kindness; through the perfection of application, there is non-dwelling with the five hindrances—namely, sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt;
and through having cultivated the antidotes, there is the destruction of all latent tendencies, such as ignorance and the rest.
The eleven aspects are: the yoga of mindfulness and clear comprehension through constant meditative composure; pure robes and other requisites for use through pure conduct;
and the non-occurrence of eighty thousand families of worms within the body due to being a root of virtue accepted by the entire world.
Through the purification of the roots of virtue, there is freedom from mental crookedness;
through being indifferent to gain, honor, and the like, there is the undertaking of the ascetic qualities (dhūtaguṇa) such as wearing robes made of rags from dust heaps;
and through the practice of the specific perfections such as giving, there is the absence of their opposites, such as stinginess and the violation of ethical discipline.

The six aspects are: proceeding through the yoga of the perfection of wisdom without contradicting the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) by way of encompassing all phenomena; and the longing for the hells for the sake of others because one has made the realm of sentient beings one's own.
Furthermore, there is the state of not being led by others due to having attained conviction in the true nature of phenomena.
There are two aspects: the recognition of a Māra who teaches a counterfeit path as being Māra himself, due to having realized the skillful means of Buddhahood;
and the aspect of being rejoiced in by the Buddhas in all practices through the purity of the three spheres.

It should be understood that a Bodhisattva established in the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and Supreme Mundane Dharmas does not turn back from unexcelled enlightenment by means of these twenty signs, respectively.

Immediately after [the description of] the characteristics of irreversibility pertaining to the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he states the characteristics of irreversibility on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) with one intermediate verse:

"The six moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) in the path of seeing—these five and five [moments] should be known as the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s irreversibility. (Abhis 4.46)

Thus, the sixteen moments beginning with the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), accessed by way of the truths such as suffering, constitute the characteristic of irreversibility for a bodhisattva abiding on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
If one asks what the characteristics of these moments and their aspects (*ākāra*) are, he states the aspects in five intermediate verses:
"The turning away from the perception of form and so forth, firmness of mind toward the two inferior [vehicles]..."
The turning away from these two vehicles and the complete exhaustion of the factors of meditation and so forth.
Lightness of body and mind, the skillful means for engaging in sensual desires, constant practice of celibacy, and the purity of livelihood. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.48)

In the aggregates and so forth, in obstacles, in the accumulations, in that which possesses the sense faculties and so forth, in battle, and in stinginess and so forth—there is no "not" [in the context] of application and devoted application. (Abhis 4.49)
The negation of dwelling, the non-apprehension of even the subtle dharma, certainty regarding one's own stage, and abiding in the three stages. (Abhis 4.50)
The renunciation of life for the sake of the Dharma—these sixteen moments are the signs of irreversibility for the wise one established on the path of seeing. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 4.51.
Thus: by means of the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), there is the turning away from the realization of phenomena such as form;

by means of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas and others, there is firmness in the unsurpassed thought of awakening (*anuttarabodhicitta*); and by means of the practice of the distinguished teachings of the Mahāyāna, there is the turning back of the mind toward the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Through the power of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), there arises the abandonment of the factors of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); thus, there are exactly four aspects of suffering.
By being free from unwholesomeness, there is lightness of body and mind; by the power of skill in means for subduing sentient beings, there is the enjoyment of desires without attachment.

Constant practice of celibacy through the vision of the defects of sense objects, and complete purity of livelihood and requisites by way of the qualities of a true person— these are the four aspects of the origin [of suffering].
Furthermore, the prohibition of dwelling in the pursuit of yoga consists in not engaging in the application to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases due to abiding in emptiness.

There are four aspects of cessation (*nirodha*): first, because opposing factors have been cast out, there is the prohibition of dwelling in the application and pursuit of those dharmas that obstruct realization, as previously described;

second, because the faults of conceptual construction have been fully understood, there is the prohibition of dwelling in the discourse, application, and pursuit of the accumulations for enlightenment such as giving and so forth, as previously described;

third, because the grasped object and the grasping subject are to be abandoned, there is the prohibition of dwelling in the application and pursuit of battles concerning the city of the sense-faculties and their bases, as previously described. These constitute the four aspects of cessation.

Through the realization of the distinctions between generosity and the other perfections, there is the cessation of dwelling in the habitual practice of attachment to stinginess, immorality, and so forth;
through the fact that all phenomena have the nature of the three gates of liberation, there is the non-apprehension of even an atom-sized phenomenon as an object of knowledge;
and through the attainment of firm conviction, there is the state of remaining correctly determined within the three levels whose nature consists of the three types of omniscience.
Because of being devoted to solitude, there is the relinquishing of life for the sake of the dharmas such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); thus, there are four aspects of the path.

In this way, when the moments of patience and knowledge are correctly realized through sixteen aspects, they produce their own corresponding effects—which are the objects of others' understanding—such as the turning away from the notions of form and so forth, which are comprised within the pure mundane subsequent consciousness that is free from the aspects of grasped object and grasping subject. Therefore...
These are the characteristics of a bodhisattva who is irreversible while abiding on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

It is stated figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) to make it known that the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of yogins everywhere corresponds exactly to their realization (*adhigama*), except insofar as it is driven by the purpose of training sentient beings (*sattvavinaya*);
otherwise, how could the moments (*kṣaṇa*) experienced individually within the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) of a yogin serve as characteristics for the understanding of others?

Immediately following that, although the characteristics of one who is irreversible while abiding on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) exist, [the author] first specifies that path of cultivation according to the logical principle that "cognition of the qualified object does not arise unless the qualification has been grasped," stating:
"The path of cultivation is profound; profundity consists of emptiness and so forth.
Freedom from the extremes of superimposition and denial—that is profundity. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.52)
Thus: in emptiness and so forth, there is no form and so forth, nor is emptiness and so forth anything other than that.
This state of being free from the extremes of superimposition and denial, respectively, is the profundity of emptiness and so forth.
Because it is conjoined with such profundity, the path of cultivation is profound.
Having thus indicated the qualifier, he states the qualified object:

"Reflection, deliberation, and profound meditation constitute the path of cultivation repeatedly, within the factors of penetration, on the path of vision, and indeed on the path of cultivation. (Abhis 4.53)

Thus, through the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, or through the wisdom occurring in the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there occur repeated reflections, weighings, and contemplations upon the meanings taught in the three factors of penetration (*nirvedhāṅga*) and so forth; these constitute the continuous [practice] on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

If it is asked how many types there are of that [affliction], he says: "Because it is continuous, it is held to be ninefold in its modes, through the further division of the weak, medium, and intense into [their own] weak and so forth. (Abhis 4.54)

Thus, considering that Bodhisattvas have conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*), just as gross darkness is dispelled by subtle light and subtle [darkness] by intense [light], there are respective weak, medium, and intense divisions for each of the weak,

medium, and intense conceptualizations; and likewise, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there are respective weak, medium, and intense divisions for each of their weak, medium, and intense antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

Because there is a distinction between the antidotes to conceptual construction according to the gates of the characteristics and aspects of emptiness, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) exists as ninefold in a continuous stream throughout the nine stages, beginning with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If it is asked, "How can it be ninefold when there is a manifold division based on the statement that each individual aspect of those various Mothers of the Victors (*jinajananī*) gives rise to incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless merit? he says:
Designations such as "incalculable" and so forth are not tenable from the perspective of ultimate truth;
they are accepted by the Sage only conventionally, as being the natural outflow of compassion.

Thus, these expressions—designations such as "incalculable," "immeasurable," and "limitless"—which are by nature verbal utterances, are applied to a single reality through various forms produced in dependence upon conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Therefore, they are incapable of establishing a differentiation in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) characterized as previously described from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

However, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), they are by nature the phenomena of teaching, being the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the dharmadhātu, which is itself of the nature of non-referential great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*).
Just as the aforementioned explanations are intended by the Tathāgata to reveal the arising of great fruit for foolish people, so too a plurality [of teachings] does not result [for the Tathāgata].

Anticipating the objection that—since emptiness is characterized by the absence of any addition of excellence—it performs no function whatsoever even for a person of dull intellect, he says: "Decrease and increase are not applicable to a reality that is beyond verbal expression."
What is lacking by the path called cultivation, and what has been attained?

Since the reality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-svarūpa*), which is the intended object of the path, is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and thus inexpressible as being either identical to, other than, both, or neither [the subject], there can be no cultivation of excellence (*bhāvanātiśaya*). Consequently, the sequential disappearance of the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and the arising of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are not tenable. If this is so, what is it about the nature of the adverse factors that is abandoned by the path designated as "cultivation"?
Furthermore, if it is argued that since the nature of purification has already been attained, nothing at all is being produced, and therefore it is simply not to be mentioned— this is not so.
And thus it has been said:
"Just as awakening is, so too is this [attainment] the accomplisher of the desired goal;
awakening has the characteristic of suchness, and that [attainment] is also considered to have that same characteristic. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.57)

Thus, just as awakening— which is the nature of suchness (tathatā) characterized by the imparting of the unsurpassed, and which has the Buddha-nature consisting of the Dharmakāya and so forth as its essence—

is the accomplisher of the desired object for those to be trained through its mere sovereignty, by way of generating a mind in which a distinguished object appears in accordance with their merit and knowledge; in the same way, this path as well— though it is of the character of suchness and is realized through cultivation by the removal of adventitious stains— performs the function of the desired object on the level of conventional reality.
From the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), however, the very absence of decrease and increase is accepted; thus, because non-application itself constitutes application, there is no fault.
Anticipating the objection that "in this case, causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) would not be possible conventionally (saṃvṛtyā)," he says:
"Awakening (bodhi) is not joined with the preceding mind, nor with the subsequent one."

Thus, because in each individual moment of mind— whether preceding or succeeding— the entire range of objects that produce a Buddha’s awakening, such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), does not appear, awakening cannot be achieved by a single [moment of] mind. Furthermore, since it is stated that "sentient beings possess a continuum of a single consciousness," it is impossible for awakening to be achieved even by multiple moments of mind appearing simultaneously as phenomena that produce the desired object.

It is not [appropriate] that [the agent] consists of a series of many preceding and succeeding moments of mind, which have as their nature the realization of everything from the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) that bring about unsurpassed enlightenment;
for these arise and perish without any continuity (*niranvaya*), and thus lack mutual connection.
How then is it an effective agent (*arthakriyākārī*)? It is so by way of generating a mind in which a specific object appears.
No, because that is incorrect. Thus it is said:
"By means of the analogy of the lamp, the profound nature of phenomena is eightfold. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.58)

In the first moment of the meeting of the flame and the wick, because they are indistinguishable in their simultaneous arising—having arrived through the sequence of their own causal lineage—there is an absence of the relationship of fuel and burner characterized as cause and effect.

Likewise, in the second moment, at the moment of the arising of the specific flame and wick, because there would otherwise follow the consequence of eternal existence and so forth due to the absence of the first moment, there is an absence of conventional arising; thus, there is an absence of the relationship of fuel and burner characterized as cause and effect.

Even so, nevertheless, when— by way of the nature of dependent origination consisting in specific conditionality (*idampratyayatā*)— the second moment, being distinguished by a superior capacity imparted by it, arises as a particular aggregate through the force of the causal relationship, depending upon the first moment produced as something uniquely integrated and delightful only when unexamined; then [that second moment would occur].

In that case, even if destruction were causeless, because the cause and the effect undergo destruction and arising respectively at the same time and without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*), there exists the relationship of the burner and the burned.

Therefore, in the first moment, the wick is not burned without depending on the second flame; likewise, in the second moment, the wick is not burned without depending on the first flame. Thus, by means of the logic of the lamp example—which is intended to demonstrate that two successive moments function toward a single object—[the relationship is established].

Just as in the preceding moment, the attainment of enlightenment is logically possible because, depending upon the initial consciousness—which manifests a few specific factors that bring about awakening—there arises a subsequent consciousness manifesting a distinguished object that exceeds those manifestations. Furthermore, by means of this very same illustration, the eightfold profound nature of reality is to be understood; this is for the purpose of explaining the characteristics of irreversibility for Bodhisattvas abiding on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Explaining the eightfold profundity regarding that subject, he says: "Profundity exists in arising and in cessation, in suchness, in the object of knowledge, in knowledge, in conduct, and in non-dual skillful means. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.59)

Thus, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the production of a distinguished object accessible through cultivation, which arises neither from preceding and succeeding moments nor by way of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Cessation (*nirodha*) is the fact that the arising of all phenomena is, in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), extinguished because it is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Suchness (*tathatā*) is the non-realization of that [Suchness], even while practicing with respect to suchness in all states.

It should be understood that the practice of the various kinds of giving and so forth consists of all phenomena whose intrinsic nature is suchness (*tathatā*). Knowledge is the realization that non-seeing itself is seeing by way of the form of suchness. Conduct is the realization that non-practicing anywhere is itself practicing by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Non-duality is that in which all accomplishments are achieved within the nature of non-duality.
Skillful means is the non-attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood despite the complete perfection of all accumulations.
Profundity arises from the practice of mutually contradictory purposes through the attainment of the gateway to the inconceivable liberation.
Thus, the irreversible learner has been described with their characteristics.
Having attained the qualities that constitute the equipment for a learner, they strive for the attainment of Buddhahood through the equality of existence and peace.
Therefore, explaining the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as the cause for attaining Buddhahood, he says: "Because all phenomena are like a dream, there is no conceptualization of existence or peace;
thus, the refutations of objections such as the non-existence of karma are as previously stated. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.60)

Thus: because one realizes that the factors belonging to the side of the adverse, the remedial, the worldly, and the supramundane are by nature mere appearances, similar to a dream, there is no conceptualization regarding the distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
this is "equality.

Now, as for the objection: "If they are like a dream, then just as in the dream state, there would be an absence of the ten unwholesome paths of action, giving, and so forth, even in the waking state," the refutations of such objections are, according to the system of those who assert external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), due to [the nature of] momentariness.

Since it is an established tenet that "the variety of the world arises from karma," in ultimate reality no one is killed by anyone, nor is any substance seized by anyone; yet, by adopting such a position, one produces entities that contradict the continuum of activity initiated toward a particular objective, by means of the resolve to kill and so forth.
Just as unwholesome actions such as killing are established for one who possesses improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) and so forth,

in the same way, for those whose bonds of all perversions remain unbroken due to their attachment to existence and the like regarding objects that are like dreams and their corresponding referents, the refutations of that [position] and the arguments against that side have been stated elsewhere; thus it should be understood.
Furthermore, since a mind afflicted by torpor in a dream yields a result dissimilar [to that of a waking mind], the illustrative example is unestablished.

Thus, even in a dream, for one who has accumulated wholesome or unwholesome karma, there is nourishment [of that karma] during the waking state through the reinforcement of the mental engagement of the subsequent state, such as rejoicing: "Oh, what a good deed has been done!"
And therefore, because the example is not established, there is indeed the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

(10) Regarding the supreme purification of the field— thinking that one will become a Buddha in one's own buddha-field through the cultivation of the equality of both— it says immediately thereafter [the section on] the complete purification of the buddha-field:
Through the offering of purification for whatever impurity exists in the world of sentient beings, there likewise arises the purity of the receptacle world, the Buddha-field. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.61)

Purification of the buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra-viśuddhi*) is the purification achieved by means of generating, respectively, divine enjoyments and pure golden ground as the antidote to the impurities—such as hunger, thirst, stumps, and thorns—found in the two types of buddha-fields distinguished as the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
11. Skill in Means (*upāyakauśala*).

Having accomplished the purification of his own Buddha-field through skill in means (*upāyakauśala*), he must perform the work of a Buddha according to the capacity of beings; thus, he speaks of skill in means:
"His object and his application, the overcoming of adversaries, being non-abiding, according to the impulse, and possessing an uncommon characteristic. (Abhis 4.62)
Non-attachment, non-apprehension, being free from signs and aspirations, its characteristic, and its immeasurability—skill in means is tenfold. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.63)
Thus: by transcending obstructive factors, there is the overcoming of the Māras such as the gods;
by the realization of the equality of all phenomena, there is dwelling in non-abiding;
and through the fulfillment of vows, there is the accomplishment of the welfare of others according to their needs.
It is uncommon because of the thorough practice of all difficult feats;
it is the non-apprehension of any phenomenon through the purity of white dharmas;
and it is non-perception by way of the door of liberation that is emptiness.
It is signless by virtue of being the door to the signless liberation; it is wishless by virtue of being the door to the wishless liberation;
and it is the mark of irreversibility by virtue of teaching the dharmas of irreversibility preceded by questions.

Because it possesses knowledge of all objects, it is not an invalid cognition; thus, in the direct realization of the ten types of objects of the *prajñāpāramitā*, skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) consists precisely in the application of knowing the proper and improper time.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth chapter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Fifth Chapter: The Culminating Clear Realization.

1. The Signs (*liṅga*). Since the realization of one who has attained the complete awakening to all aspects reaches its ultimate excellence, the author now describes the Culminating Clear Realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), preceded by the exposition of its signs and so forth, for the sake of easy understanding.
Even within a dream, the vision of all phenomena as appearing like a dream and so forth is considered the twelvefold sign of yoga that has reached the summit. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.1)
Thus, even in the state of dreaming, through extreme habituation, there occurs the perception of all phenomena as being like dreams,
the non-arising of a mind that longs for the stages of the Śrāvakas and others,
and the vision of the Tathāgatas and so forth.
The realization of the miraculous transformations of a Buddha's supernatural power;
the arousal of the thought of enlightenment for the purpose of teaching the Dharma and so forth;
and the recollection of the elimination of the states of woe in one’s own Buddha-field, preceded by the vision of sentient beings in the hells and other realms.
The accomplishment of the empowerment of truth that pacifies the burning of cities and so forth;
the fulfillment of truthful speech that causes non-humans such as yakṣas to depart;
and personally cultivating spiritual friends through the exertion of higher knowledge.
Training in the perfection of wisdom in all its aspects,
non-attachment to all phenomena,
and drawing near to the enlightenment of a Buddha— these are the twelve types of distinctive signs of the stage of attained clear realization.
2. Increase (*vivṛddhi*; the summit and the application of the summit):
He explains the increase, asking how many kinds of increase there are for that which has been characterized by the signs:
"The measure of people in Jambudvīpa, the worship of Buddhas, merit, and so forth..."
Having made various comparisons, the increase is sixteenfold.
Thus: the superiority of worshipping as many Tathāgatas as there are sentient beings in the three-thousandfold world system beginning with Jambūdvīpa;
the mental attention toward the distinguished perfection of wisdom;
and the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
The non-apprehension of phenomena as either the object of awakening or the awakener;
the excellence of distinction through the practice of the ten wholesome paths of action up to the formless attainments; and approaching all the assemblies of devas.
The eight kinds of merit consist of: overcoming all Māras and attaining a status equal to that of those who resemble the Teacher;
furthermore, there is training purified in every way by skillful means.
The transformation into the lineage of a Buddha,
which is the cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood,
consists in the non-arising of thoughts that are contrary to the perfections.
The non-arising of the mind through the attainment of the yoga of form and so forth;
the knowledge that encompasses all perfections;
and the acquisition of all prosperity.
The state of being near to perfect enlightenment constitutes another eight types of merit.

By making various analogies—such as the offering of flowers and so forth—to the worship of the Buddha, there occurs an increase consisting of sixteen stages through a progressive excellence of distinction.
3. *Nirūḍhi* (the stage of patience and the application of the summits).
Having thus described its increase, he speaks in order to explain its "consolidation" (nirūḍhi), which is characterized by reaching the limit of becoming one's own nature:
"The supreme fulfillment of the qualities of the three types of omniscience, without abandoning the welfare of sentient beings, is called consolidation. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.3)

Thus, by the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) alone, in this state of non-conceptual realization (*nirvikalpādhigama*), through the manifestation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and so forth,

there is the unsurpassed fulfillment and firm establishment of the aforementioned factors of the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*)— beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)— such as the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) and others, characterized by not abandoning the welfare of sentient beings.

4. *Cittasaṃsthitiḥ* (the application of the summit, known as the supreme mundane dharmas): Having thus become firmly rooted through stabilization, there is the "settling of the mind" characterized by its becoming steady; thus he speaks of the settling of the mind:
"It is comparable to [the merit of] a thousandfold world-system of four continents, or a two-thousandfold or three-thousandfold [world-system]."
By means of the abundance of merit thus produced, meditative concentration is fully proclaimed.

Thus, according to the principle that it is possible to measure the quantity of something whose magnitude is conceivable by means of a standard of weight (*pala*), [the Buddha] has described the stabilization of the mind characterized by meditative absorption (*samādhi*)— which is distinguished from all the four continents and the triple-thousandfold world systems, and from all the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth that consist of the nature of concentration, merit, and wisdom— by making separate comparisons for each of them on account of its vastness of merit that transcends all measurement.
These signs and so forth should be understood as being, respectively, the nature of the four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), beginning with "heat" (*ūṣman*).
5. The Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*): [The Application of the Summit (*mūrdhaprayoga*)].
Immediately following the aids to penetration is the path of seeing.
In this context, there are four kinds of opposing factors (vipakṣa) together with their antidotes (pratipakṣa).

First, regarding the opposing factors, he states that there are two types of conceptualization of the apprehended object (grāhyavikalpa), each consisting of nine aspects: those pertaining to the process of engagement (pravṛtti) and those pertaining to the process of cessation (nivṛtti).
The two conceptualizations regarding the apprehended object should be understood as having the nature of non-corresponding objects.

Thus, the two sides of engagement and withdrawal—which have as their intrinsic nature the non-perception and perception [of objects]—are to be understood respectively by Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and others in the form of the taking up and abandoning of phenomena. These are the two types of conceptualization of the object (*grāhyavikalpa*), which, like the afflictions, are adverse factors (*vipakṣa*). Because they function without being bound to a real entity and because they appear falsely, they do not correspond to the actual nature of things; they should be known to each consist of nine varieties according to the distinctions of their objects.
Having thus indicated the two sides of the conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*), he states the two types of conceptualization of the apprehender (*grāhaka-vikalpa*):
"The conceptualizations of sentient beings as substantially real (*dravyasat*) and as nominally real (*prajñaptisat*) are considered the apprehenders.
Through the distinction between ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), each of these two consists of nine types. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.6)
If the two objects do not exist as such, of what could they be considered the apprehenders?
Thus, their characteristic is emptiness by way of the state of being an apprehender. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.7)

Thus, the two types of subject-grasping conceptualization (*grāhakavikalpa*)—which respectively have as their basis the person who is substantially real (*dravyasat*) and the person who is nominally real (*prajñaptisat*), namely the ordinary worldling and the noble one—are the adversaries (*vipakṣa*) because they act as obstacles. Each of these is of nine varieties according to the distinction of their objects.
When the two objects that have become the state of being grasped do not exist in the manner of being graspable, then those two are not the graspers of anything at all.
Because these two appear erroneously as having a nature distinct from the form of the grasper, they should be understood as not having the true nature of their respective objects.
How is the first type of conceptualization of the graspable—the basis for the process of engagement—ninefold? To this he says:
"In regard to intrinsic nature, the lineage, the practice, and the full attainment..."
Regarding the non-erroneousness of the object of knowledge, and regarding the antidote and the discordant factor. // Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.8 //
Regarding one's own attainment, the agent, their activity, and the fruit of that activity, conceptualization based on the side of engagement is considered to be ninefold. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.9)

Thus: [it exists] in that which is by nature the non-comprehension of the isolated within the isolated; in the certain lineage of the Buddha through entry into the stages beginning with the Immovable (*acalā*);
and in the full realization of the path of seeing and so forth through practice that is like an illusion (*māyopama*).
In the case of the object of non-erroneous cognition, which consists of mere appearance;
in the case of the counter-position and its opposite, characterized by being respectively to be adopted or rejected based on their qualities and defects;
and in the case of one's own realization, which is free from all stains.

One should engage [in these practices] as something to be adopted because they are faultless, in terms of: distancing oneself from the levels of the Śrāvakas and others by means of their inferiority; performing activities for the benefit of sentient beings through the manifestation of emanations according to their inclinations; and the fruit of the activity of establishing all beings in nirvāṇa by the power of correct skillful means.

Thus, the first type of conceptualization of the apprehended object, which has the side of active involvement as its basis, is considered to consist of nine varieties that are to be abandoned during the stage of application on the path of seeing.
How is it that the second type of conceptualization of the apprehended object, which has the side of cessation as its basis, is also ninefold? It is said:
because of falling into existence or peace, and because of deficiency in realization.
And when there is an absence of grasping, or when it has become deficient, or when it has reached the [correct] practice. // Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.10 //

Regarding the reliance on others for understanding, the failure to turn back from what has been undertaken, partiality, and diversity; and regarding delusion concerning the state of abiding and the point of departure. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.11)
And regarding the alternative of following behind—this ninefold conceptualization is based on the side of cessation and arises from the minds of the Śrāvakas and others. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.12)
Thus, there is deficiency in realization due to falling into either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; there is an absence of being fully embraced due to a lack of spiritual friends and skillful means;
and there is a deficiency in the path due to its not being an antidote to all cognitive obscurations.

In the case of relying on the instruction of the Tathāgatas and others, there is the state of following the conviction of another; in the case of the cessation of the objective, there is the non-occurrence of the greatness of mind such as being foremost among all sentient beings;
and in the case of the activity of the limited path, there is its nature as an antidote to the obscuration of afflictions.
Because it possesses apprehension, there is the diversity of attaining the first fruit and so forth;
because all latent tendencies of ignorance have not been abandoned, there is the lack of knowledge regarding staying and going;

and because it encompasses all aspects of the Mahāyāna, there is the subsequent following after all forms of omniscience and all nirvāṇas. Therefore, one must effect the cessation [of this state] by way of its being a faulty object of apprehension.

Thus, this second type of conceptualization of the apprehended object (*grāhyavikalpa*), which is based on the side of cessation (*nivṛttipakṣa*) and arises from being adopted by the mental continuums of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, is considered to be abandoned in nine ways during the state of the activity of the mind and mental factors on the Bodhisattvas' path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

How is the first type of conceptualization of the apprehending subject (*grāhakavikalpa*), which is based on the person who is a real entity (*dravyasat*)—namely, an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*)—ninefold? To this he says:

The first should be known as the grasper (grāhaka) in the grasping and releasing [of objects], in the mental attention (manaskriyā), and in the conjunction of the three elements (dhātu). Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.13.

In the case of the locus, of adherence, of the designation of the entity of phenomena, of attachment, of the antidote, and of the destruction of rebirth according to one's wish; (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.14)
Thus: conventionally, there is grasping and releasing like an illusion;
in reality, there is mental engagement through non-mental-engagement; and by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is adherence to the three realms.
In emptiness through non-abiding;
in all attachment through non-attachment to things;
and in the designation of all phenomena through their substantial existence.
Due to attachment to the knowledge of reality, there is attachment preceded by non-attachment; due to the counteragent being a counteragent to the cultivation of equanimity;

and due to the obstruction of proceeding according to one's wish because the perfection of wisdom has not been correctly understood—through such attachment to ultimate entities, the first type of subject-object conceptualization (*grāhakavikalpa*) is ninefold during the stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"It is considered to be abandoned.
How is the second type of conceptualization of a grasper, which has a person existing as a mere designation (*prajñaptisat*) as its basis, ninefold? He says:
"With respect to the non-departure according to the instruction, and with respect to the determination of what is the path and what is not the path."
Regarding cessation and arising, and regarding the union with and separation from entities. // Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.15 //

When there is the station, the destruction of the lineage, the absence of prayer and causes, and the perception of an adversary, there is another conceptualization which is the grasper. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.16)

Thus: [there is] non-emergence from the aforementioned objectives by way of the emergence of the Śrāvakas and others; the determination that other paths are not the path due to the absence of one's own desired path;
and arising and cessation by way of the conventional relationship between cause and effect.
Through the appearance of one another without interval, there is the conjunction and disjunction of all things;
through the likeness of a bird situated in the sky, there is the locus of form and so forth;
and through the gateway of the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and so on, there is the destruction of the lineages of the *śrāvakas* and others.
When there is an absence of aspiration due to the non-existence of any dharma distinct from suchness;

when there is an absence of causes by relying on ultimate truth; and when, despite the habitual nature of stinginess, one perceives objects such as adversaries or Māras through an adherence to the existence of conceptual designations.

The second type of conceptualization regarding the subject (*grāhakavikalpa*) is held to be of nine kinds and is to be abandoned during the state of the functioning of the mind and mental factors on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Having thus explained the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) along with their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) on the path of seeing, he states an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*) to demonstrate the reason why the path of seeing is desired as being accompanied by that which brings about the accomplishment of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*):
The manifestation of others in enlightenment and the entrustment for its sake;
the cause immediately preceding that attainment is characterized by an abundance of merit. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.17)
Thus: first is the establishing of others in the realization of the characteristics that will be explained hereafter by demonstrating the paths of seeing and so forth;
second is the entrusting of the Perfection of Wisdom to others for the very sake of their awakening, by means of correctly [teaching] the texts, their meanings, and so on;
and third is the characteristic of merit consisting in one’s own abundant cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom and other practices, which is the immediate cause for the attainment of awakening.

What, then, is this Great Awakening (mahābodhi) for the sake of which the path of seeing, accompanied by the causes as previously described, is intended? He explains Great Awakening with an intermediate verse:
"Awakening is said to be the knowledge of the destruction and non-arising of the impurities;
because of their absence of destruction and their non-arising, these [impurities] relate to the objects of knowledge respectively. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.18)
Thus: regarding the stains of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions, which are conceptually constructed as either arisen or unarisen—
since no phenomenon exists that is separate from the *dharmadhātu*,

and because there is an absence of cessation and arising for those things whose nature is the *dharmadhātu* like that of space, due to the lack of any entity established by means of [logical] criteria such as unity or plurality, intrinsic nature, effect, cause, or valid cognition.

Alternatively, like a lotus in the sky, because there is respectively no destruction or arising of impurities, Great Awakening (mahābodhi)— which consists of the knowledge of non-destruction and non-arising, is characterized by the non-erroneous realization of all phenomena, and is essentially the Dharma-body and so forth— is thus designated. Since this is so, those who, with the intention that entities are destroyed, hold the cognition "it is destroyed" when [impurities] have been exhausted, [claim] that to be the "knowledge of destruction" (kṣayajñāna).
And with the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) that phenomena are non-arisen, they describe the knowledge that "the non-arisen is non-arisen" as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
They also describe awakening (*bodhi*) as the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
Because these [others] lack the knowledge of destruction and non-arising, this [awakening] is not possible for them; thus he says in an intermediate verse:

When primordial nature (prakṛti) has not been suppressed by the path called "vision," what mass of conceptual constructions has been destroyed, or what has reached the state of non-arising? (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.19)

Thus: since the nature (*prakṛti*), which is in the ultimate sense the form of suchness (*tathatā*), is unceasing—characterized by cessation through the destruction of what has arisen and the prevention of what has not yet arisen—which [phenomenon] consisting of conceptual construction and so forth could have arisen, and which could have remained unarisen as something characterized by non-arising, for you who adhere to false entities by the power of the path of seeing?
For there is nothing at all.
Therefore, the intention is that our own view alone must be accepted.

Otherwise, if one were to admit the existence of real entities (*dharmas*), the Blessed One’s total abandonment of the obscurations of conceptual construction, afflictions, and the knowable would become a matter of great wonder; thus he says in an intermediate verse:
"And yet there is the existence of entities, and the destruction of obscurations regarding the knowable."
That which is described by others as belonging to the Teacher, I am amazed by it here. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.20)
Thus it is said. For there, by contemplating that there is no self because it is empty of arising and ceasing, one abandons the dogmatic adherence to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*).

Having perceived the aggregates and so forth—which are devoid of such a self—as dependently originated and characterized by the nature of arising and ceasing, and reflecting that "this is mind-only and no external object exists" due to the rule of the simultaneous perception of blue and the cognition thereof, one [remains] with an un-abandoned dogmatic adherence to the aspect of the grasper (*grāhakākāra*) within the mind.

Having set aside the adherence to external objects and having reflected that "in the absence of the grasped, there is the absence of the grasper," one then discards even that mere-cognition (*vijñaptimātra*) characterized by the aspect of the grasper. Having ascertained that non-dual gnosis alone is, in reality, the true nature of existence,

one realizes that even this, because it is dependently originated, is devoid of intrinsic nature like an illusion, and in its ultimate reality, is free from all conceptualizations such as absolute existence or non-existence.

By cultivating this, when the power of cultivation is perfected, just like the cognition of gems, silver, and so forth, there arises in some a non-conceptual cognition that manifests as an illusion-like self, in which all causes of error have been dispelled; being personally realized in some way, upon its production, the yogi correctly abandons the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Otherwise, if momentary phenomena— whether they be of the nature of cognition alone or characterized as objects of cognition— were to exist in an ultimate sense, just as space always maintains the nature of being a mere absence of substance and thus possesses a nature that cannot be added to or removed, then nothing could be effected by the cultivation of their antidotes, just as nothing can be done to space.

Therefore, because the misconception of clinging to existence has not been abandoned, the Blessed One’s total abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the fact that others accept the existence of phenomena—these two mutually contradictory positions being accepted [simultaneously]—would be a cause for astonishment. Having thus refuted the position of existence, he states the position of the established [truth] through an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*), so that those seeking liberation might firmly adopt this very [position] by strengthening the position of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*): [The intermediate verse: "Since the Blessed One has abandoned all obscurations, And since the existence of things is accepted by others, This [acceptance of both] is a cause for wonder, For these two are mutually contradictory. In this way, having rejected the side of existence and by means of strengthening the side of the absence of intrinsic nature, he shows that this alone must be accepted by those desiring liberation.
Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is, and he who sees reality is liberated. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.21)

Thus, because liberation is impossible through such adherence to the existence of entities, one must not perform the removal or addition of any dharma—that is, the forms of denial (*apavāda*) or superimposition (*samāropa*).

Rather, this very dependently originated [reality], which is true by way of conventional truth, should be examined as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and so forth in its form as matter (*rūpa*) and the rest.
And in this way, just as one illusory elephant defeats another illusory elephant, the seer of reality is liberated through the cessation of error.

Having thus stated these incidental matters, he describes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) under discussion: "The mutual synthesis of each one of those [perfections], beginning with generosity, which is comprised within patience (*kṣānti*), is here the path of seeing consisting of a single moment. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.22)

Thus, regarding each of the six perfections beginning with giving, the mutual inclusion of all perfections within each one—such as giving—is here the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the "summit" realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*). It is comprised by the acceptance of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*), manifested through the purity of the three spheres (*trimandalaviśuddhi*), and produced from thirty-six aspects. And in this [path of seeing]...

When [this realization] has arisen, through the abandonment of one hundred and eight conceptualizations of subject and object—each divided according to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and each consisting of four types of conceptualization and nine modes—the abandonment of the one hundred and eight afflictions of the *vāsanās* that generate those conceptualizations is perceived as the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*).
To gain mastery over this, one cultivates it again and again; thus he says in an intermediate verse:
Having entered that samādhi, he then contemplates dependent origination in the lion’s stretch, both in direct and reverse order. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.23)

Thus, having attained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the yogi—being free from the fear of the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—enters the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "The Lion’s Yawn.

Thereafter, he examines dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in its forward order, beginning with "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*), and in its reverse order, beginning with "from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇanirodho jātinirodhāt*).
This is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), specifically the practice of the summit (*mūrdhaprayoga*).

Having thus explained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and since the abandonment of opposing factors (*vipakṣaprahāṇa*) and so forth are easily understood as being preceded by the practice of the basis (*ādhārapratipatti*), he states the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as that basis: "Taking the consciousness belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāpta*) as the limit, having gone through and returned from the nine meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—including cessation (*nirodha*)—in two ways, [the non-concentrated consciousness (*asamāhita-vijñāna*) arises]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.24)

By skipping over one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight [stages], there is the attainment by leaping (*avaskandasamāpatti*), which is the cessationless and incomparable state. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 5.25.

Thus, the bodhisattvas, having proceeded from the first dhyāna up to cessation (*nirodha*), and then having returned from cessation back down to the first dhyāna—in this manner, by means of the two sequences of forward and reverse order—they traverse and return from the nine attainments characterized by the four dhyānas, the four formless states (*ārūpya*), and cessation. Having again entered the first dhyāna and emerged from it, they enter cessation;
and in this way, proceeding up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they enter cessation.

Then, having emerged from that [attainment], taking the immediately preceding attainment as an object, one establishes consciousness belonging to the desire realm in the form of a boundary; then, emerging through the power of skillful means, one brings that very same non-concentrated consciousness to manifestation.

From there, one enters cessation, then the non-concentrated state, then cessation—omitting one [instance]; then the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, then the non-concentrated state; then omitting two [instances], one enters the sphere of nothingness, then the non-concentrated state.

In this way, having abandoned up to eight [stages]— from the first dhyāna and then the non-concentrated state— one proceeds by skipping over dissimilar doors as far as the attainment of cessation (*anirodhasamāpatti*). Having brought face-to-face the "leap-over attainment" (*avaskandasamāpatti*), characterized by mastery, which goes in an unequal manner, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) comes into being.
Having thus explained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the fourfold adverse factor (*vipakṣa*) to be abandoned therein must now be stated.
First, he states the conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhyavikalpa*):
"With respect to the concise and the detailed, with respect to the Buddhas' assistance and non-assistance..."
When there is an absence of qualities regarding the three times, on the threefold path to the supreme good.
"This is the single conceptualization of the apprehended object, which has the aspects of application as its domain.

Thus, [the Buddha taught] the summary of the Dharma out of favor toward sentient beings who delight in brevity, and the expansion of the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings who delight in detail.
Due to the non-implementation of the prescribed meanings, there is a lack of the Buddha's assistance and protection;
due to the state of having arisen and then ceased, there is an absence of the qualities of the path of preparation;
and due to the deficiency of the causes for correct origination, there is an absence of the qualities of the path of seeing.
Because of the non-existence of future things, there is an absence of qualities on the path of cultivation;
because of the pacification of error and so forth, there is [an absence] on the preparatory path to nirvāṇa;
and because of the actualization of emptiness, there is [an absence] on the path of seeing.

And on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), by way of realizing the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), the first conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhyavikalpa*) is to be abandoned in this state; having thus first described the ninefold object of that preparatory stage of the path of cultivation, he states the second conceptualization of the apprehended:
"The second is considered the object of the activity of mind and mental factors" (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.27).

The non-arising of the mind, lack of mental attention toward the seat of enlightenment, mental attention toward the Lesser Vehicle, and lack of mental attention toward perfect enlightenment [are the obstacles]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.28)

In the path of cultivation, conceptual construction should be understood as being fourfold: that which consists in cultivation, that which consists in non-cultivation, its opposite, and that which is unreal. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.29)

Thus: due to the absence of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth, there is the non-arising of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); due to the lack of merit based on the sublime object of the Buddha, there is the failure to attend to the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*); and due to belonging to the lineage of the hearers (*śrāvakagotra*), there is the mental engagement with that [hearer] vehicle.

Because of belonging to the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhas, there is the failure to bring that vehicle to manifestation; because of the lack of practice in the perfection of wisdom, there is the failure to attend to perfect enlightenment;
and because of having apprehension (*sopalambha*), there is cultivation, while because of being without apprehension (*nirupalambha*), there is non-cultivation.
Because non-apprehension is itself non-apprehensible, there is neither cultivation nor non-cultivation;

and because of the adherence to the contrary, which constitutes being unreal, this is the second conceptualization of the apprehended object (*grāhyavikalpa*). In that state—namely, during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) where the mind and mental factors are active as that which is to be abandoned—it is ninefold in its objective domain.
Having thus indicated the second [type], he states the first, the conceptualization of the grasper (grāhakavikalpa):

The first grasper should be known as having the designation of a sentient being as its object; it consists of the investigation of attachment to the non-emptiness of the designation of phenomena. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.30)

And it is proclaimed [as an offense] regarding the performance of a ritual act, regarding the three vehicles, regarding the impurity of a religious gift, or regarding the violation of the conduct. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.31)
Thus, when existence is designated through the impossibility of a substantial entity,
and all phenomena are designated as being mere appearances;
Because of its omnipresence, when the phenomena such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are empty;

because of the failure to abandon attachment in every way, there is clinging to phenomena (*dharmasakti*); and through the realization of the absence of intrinsic nature, there is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
In the case of making a presentation of the entities instead of making a presentation of the summary;
in the case of departure via the three vehicles because of the perception of form and so forth;
and in the case of the purity of the sacrificial fee because of not practicing correctly.

And regarding the non-disturbance of the practice through the negation of the apprehension of giving and so forth, as before, there is a ninefold conceptualization of the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*) which is the object during the stage of preparation for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Having thus explained the first [type], he states the second conceptualization of the grasper:
"The other is ninefold, having the designation of a sentient being and its cause as its object."
That which is connected to the path of cultivation is the adverse element, because it obstructs that [path].

Thus [ends the section]. The second type of conceptualization regarding the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*) is the adverse factor (*vipakṣa*). Its object consists of the mere appearance of the designation of a sentient being (*sattvaprajñapti*) and the causes for its establishment; because it is to be abandoned by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is connected with that [path] and is of nine types.
If one asks how it is of nine types, he explains by means of two intermediate verses (*antaraśloka*):

Regarding the three types of omniscience, there is [the obstruction] corresponding to their respective threefold obscurations, as well as [the obstructions] regarding the association with and dissociation from the path to peace, suchness, and so forth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.33)

The final conceptualization is considered to be the delusion regarding inequality, suffering and so forth, the intrinsic nature of the afflictions, and the absence of duality. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.34)
Thus: due to the non-comprehension of all aspects, there is the delusion regarding the obscuration to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

due to the non-comprehension of all paths, there is the delusion regarding the obscuration to the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*); and due to the non-comprehension of all things, there is the delusion regarding the obscuration to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Through the lack of thorough knowledge of the perfection of wisdom, there is delusion regarding all peaceful paths;
through the lack of thorough knowledge of suchness and the objects of knowledge such as form and so forth, there is delusion regarding the conjunction and disjunction of suchness and so forth;
and through the lack of thorough knowledge of the true nature of Māra and others, there is delusion regarding inequality.
Due to grasping at the literal meaning of words, there is delusion regarding the truths such as suffering;
due to not fully understanding the nature of passion and other afflictions, there is delusion regarding the fundamental nature of the afflictions;

and due to not fully understanding the characteristics of the grasped object and the grasping subject, there is delusion regarding non-duality. As before, the final type of subject-object conceptualization consists of nine varieties that serve as objects during the stage when the mind and mental factors of the path of cultivation are active.
Thus it is considered.

It should be understood that, upon the abandonment of those factors which are the adversaries of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the fourfold antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is likewise differentiated according to their distinctions. Just as before, at the very moment the one hundred and eight conceptualizations are abandoned, the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) comprised within them are also abandoned; thus, all perfections of qualities take recourse in the bodhisattva abiding on the path of cultivation. This is stated in two intermediate verses (*antaraśloka*): [The verses follow] In brief, it is said: "By means of the fourfold antidote, there is the abandonment of the one hundred and eight conceptualizations; simultaneously, through the abandonment of the one hundred and eight afflictions contained therein, all perfections of qualities take recourse in the bodhisattva abiding on the path of cultivation. Thus it is taught.

When these afflictions have been exhausted, the perfections of virtue—which accomplish the happiness of the world in all its aspects—seem as if they have been breathing a long sigh of relief. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.35)
All [virtues] resort to that Great Being with their full force, abounding in desired fruits, just as rivers flow into the great ocean. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.36)
Thus, through the cultivation of the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when these types of fourfold conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)— which act as afflictions— are exhausted,
all the perfections of qualities (*guṇasampad*) comprised within the three vehicles, having attained a sense of relief and inspiration due to the absence of obstruction,
become capable of producing every form of happiness for the world through their dependence on compassion, by way of approaching [the goal] in every respect.

Just as rivers resort to the great ocean, so do [the perfections] resort to the Bodhisattva abiding on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), who possesses the splendor of having attained the fruits that are the ultimate limit of excellence;
this is the "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), also known as the "peak application" (*mūrdha-prayoga*).
Immediately following the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), he explains the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga):

Having established the inhabitants of the three-thousandfold world system in the excellence of the attainments of the disciples and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas], as well as in the bodhisattva’s stage (nyāma), [the merit] is comparable to that of the wholesome [deeds]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.37)

Having performed [these deeds], through the abundance of merit, immediately after the attainment of Buddhahood, there is the "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) samādhi; and that is omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.38)

Thus: having established all sentient beings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system upon the path (nyāma) of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, one takes as a comparison whatever merit flows forth from that act; then, by virtue of a much greater merit even more distinguished than that, there is the state of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is Buddhahood. The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is immediately contiguous with the attainment of Buddhahood is here called the "uninterrupted absorption" (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
If one asks what its objects of focus (*ālambana*) and other characteristics are like:
By means of an intermediate verse, he states the object of focus and so forth:
"Its object of focus is non-existence, and mindfulness is considered its dominant influence;
its aspect here is tranquility, [directed] at those who speak with a stream of chatter. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.39)
Thus, for this immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), the perception of the non-existence of all phenomena is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
mindfulness is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
and primordial tranquility is its aspect (*ākāra*).

And in this matter, because it is difficult to fathom, the various misconceptions of proponents who are ignorant of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) spread forth through a succession of diverse lines of objection;
therefore, these must be refuted by means of skillful means.
The intention is that by this, its profundity has been expressed.
8. Regarding "Misconception" (*vipratipatti*, the application of the summit):
If it is asked, "What kinds of misconceptions of those with perverted minds must be dispelled so that that meditative concentration may be produced? [the following is said:]
Immediately after [discussing] meditative concentration (samādhi), he states the misconceptions regarding:

the occurrence of the object of focus, the determination of its intrinsic nature, the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects, and the ultimate truth along with the conventional. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.40)
In the application [to the three jewels], in the means together with the occasion of the Sage, in error and the true path, and in the antidote and the discordant factor; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.41.

Regarding the characteristics and the cultivation [of the path], the disputants are held to have sixteen and ten misconceptions, respectively, concerning the basis of the knowledge of all aspects. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.42)
Thus, when the objective support is established through the non-existence of both the conditioned and unconditioned realms;
when the intrinsic nature of the objective support is determined because it is entirely devoid of form;
and when there is the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects through the non-apprehension of existence and non-existence—
In the two truths of the conventional and the ultimate by virtue of having suchness as their intrinsic nature;
in the application through the non-apprehension of giving and so forth;
and in the Jewel of the Buddha due to the absence of anything to be awakened to.
Because the Jewel of the Dharma is a mere name; because the Jewel of the Saṅgha is the negation of objective supports such as form and so forth;
and because skill in means consists in the non-apprehension of giving and the other perfections.
In the realization of the Tathāgata, there is [the absence of error] regarding existence, non-existence, and both, because of the negation of their apprehension;
