regarding permanence and so forth, because of the erroneous inversion of permanence and so forth as established through conceptual proliferation;
and regarding the path, because of the failure to realize the fruit of the path that has been cultivated.
Due to the absence of relinquishment and acquisition regarding the adverse side and its counteragent;

due to the absence of a substratum (dharmin) regarding the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa); and because cultivation is untenable due to the impossibility of specific and general characteristics, the meanings of the words are mutually contradictory and thus unfit for practical application.

Having dispelled, by means of skillful means based on the two truths as appropriate, all sixteen types of misconceptions in the form of doubt— which have the aforementioned objects as their domain and are grounded in the knowledge of all aspects— and having generated a correct and complete certainty, bodhisattvas who desire what is wholesome attain the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), [having done so] for all those people who proclaim [these views] while remaining ignorant of the bodhisattva’s skillful means.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth chapter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The sixth chapter is the Chapter on the Successive Realization (*Ānupūrvikādhikāra*).

Regarding the "Successive Clear Realization" (*Anupūrvābhisamaya*): having attained the Peak Clear Realization, one now brings the objects previously realized—both individually and collectively—into their proper sequence and meditates upon them in order to consolidate that realization; thus, he speaks of the successive clear realization.

Through generosity, wisdom, and so forth up to the recollections of the Buddha and others, and by means of the nature of the non-existence of phenomena—this is considered the gradual practice. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 6.1)

Thus, by means of the complete fulfillment of all aspects of the six perfections—beginning with generosity—as manifested through the purity of the three spheres; by means of the four applications of mindfulness and so forth, which bring about the ten stages and are included within the perfection of wisdom; and by means of the seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path, which ultimately possess the characteristic of non-recollection and sequentially illuminate the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—through this threefold recollection of the Buddha.
In the same way, through the recollection of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral phenomena as before, through the recollection of the noble and irreversible community of bodhisattvas,
and likewise through the recollection of ethical discipline, renunciation, and the deities, as well as the realization of the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena such as form—
that attainment is intended here as the gradual practice.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixth chapter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The seventh chapter is the "Chapter on Enlightenment in a Single Instant.

For one who has cultivated the gradual realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*), enlightenment in a single instant (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*) occurs through the attainment of those very same [realizations] in a single moment, in order to bring them to complete mastery.
That [awakening] is also fourfold by way of its characteristics:
1. The characteristic of non-maturation (*avipāka-lakṣaṇa*).
The first momentary awakening (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*) is characterized by all dharmas, which are non-maturing and untainted (*anāsrava*), in a single moment. Thus it is said:
Because all untainted [dharmas] are subsumed even by each one individually, this realization in a single moment by the Sage through giving and so forth is to be known. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 7.1)
In the nature of the dharmadhātu— there is one entity which is the nature of all entities, and all entities have the nature of that one entity.
By whomsoever one entity is seen in its true reality, by him all entities are seen in their true reality.
According to this principle, it is not only that one thing is subsumed by many; rather,

through the knowledge of giving and so forth occurring in a single moment— which takes as its object a state free from the error of grasping at specific, fixed entities— there is the realization of the Sage, the Bodhisattva, by way of the subsumption of those dharmas characterized by the eighty minor marks (anuvyañjana) such as giving and the rest.
Indeed, this should be understood as "awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*).
If it is asked: "In that case, how can there be a synthesis of all untainted (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] within a single object of untainted knowledge?
he replies with a worldly analogy:
Just as even a single bucket at a waterwheel, when pulled by men,
moves the entire wheel all at once, so too does knowledge in a single moment.
Thus, just as even a single step taken by a person causes an entire waterwheel to turn all at once— due to the power of the prior craftsmanship of the artisan—
so too, through the power of the *dharmadhātu* impelled by previous vows, a single uncontaminated object being apprehended in one very moment causes all things of the same class to manifest.
2. The characteristic of maturation (*vipāka-lakṣaṇa*).

Having thus first explained [the first moment], the second is the momentary perfect awakening (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*) characterized by all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) abiding in the state of the nature of maturation. Thus it is said:
"When the state of the nature of maturation consists entirely of the pure."
Then, in a single moment, the perfection of wisdom gives birth to primordial gnosis.

When, through the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the antidotes and the removal of all opposing factors, the state of the natural dharma (*dharmatā*)— which constitutes the entirety of the side of purification— becomes white in nature like the moonlight of autumn due to the departure of all stains, then, because of the awakening to the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) that have reached the state of maturation in a single moment, that knowledge is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), known as "awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*).
3. The characteristic of the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇalakṣaṇa*).

Having thus explained the second [type of momentary realization], the third is the momentary realization characterized by the single-moment characteristic of all phenomena as being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇasarvadharmaikakṣaṇalakṣaṇa*). Thus he said:
"Abiding in phenomena that are like a dream, through the practice of giving and so forth..."
In a single moment, one realizes the signlessness of all phenomena.

Having previously experienced the two accumulations through the practice of all phenomena as being like a dream, and then, at the stage of realization, abiding within all phenomena such as the aggregates of grasping which have the nature of a dream, one practices the six perfections of giving and so forth. By means of the mode of discerning the forms of giving and the rest, one realizes that "all phenomena are without characteristics. Thus, in a single moment, one realizes the characteristiclessness of all phenomena, whether they are of the nature of affliction or purification.
"He knows"—thus is the single-moment perfect awakening (ekakṣaṇābhisambodha).

Having thus explained the third [awakening] characterized by non-duality, the fourth is the single-moment perfect awakening characterized by all phenomena as having the characteristic of non-duality in a single moment. Thus he said:
One does not perceive the dream nor the one who sees it through the duality of the two;
one perceives the non-dual reality of all phenomena in a single instant. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 7.5)

When a bodhisattva— having uprooted the latent tendencies for the appearance of duality through the internalization of the practice of abandoning the appearance of both [subject and object] over a continuous and long period of time— no longer perceives a dream as an object (*grāhya*) by way of subject-object engagement, nor perceives the dreamer as a subject (*grāhaka*), then he realizes in a single moment alone the non-dual reality of phenomena (*dharma-tattva*), namely that "all phenomena have such a nature. This is called "awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*).
Thus ends the commentary on the seventh chapter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The eighth chapter: The Dharmakāya.
1. The Svabhāvakāya.
For one who has realized the single-moment awakening (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), there is the realization of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāyābhisambodha*) in the second moment.
And that is fourfold, distinguished by the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and the others.
Regarding this, he says that the first is the essential body:
Those untainted phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects constitute the essential body (svābhāvikakāya) of the Sage, characterized by their intrinsic nature.
The applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth consist of gnosis; being supramundane because they have the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, they are untainted and stainless.

Since they have attained purification in every respect—characterized by natural isolation through the adventitiousness [of defilements]—their nature, which is their intrinsic essence in the form of non-arising, is realized by the Blessed Buddha, the Sage, via the supramundane path.

The *svābhāvikakāya* (essential body) is attained through the realization of all phenomena as being like an illusion, by way of a cognition that is non-artificial in the sense that it is not produced.

To explain that the remaining three bodies appear according to conventional truth (*tathyasaṃvṛti*), while in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) they are of the nature of *dharmatā*, and are established as the respective domains of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and others, manifested according to their respective inclinations (*adhimukti*): ... [the text continues] ...it is said: "It is not made," in the sense of being unconditioned; thus, the *svābhāvikakāya* is realized through the practice of understanding all phenomena as being like an illusion. As for the remaining three bodies, they appear through conventional truth, yet in the ultimate sense they are of the nature of *dharmatā*, established as the spheres of experience for Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and so forth, as manifested according to their respective convictions.

Since it is held that discernment (*viveka*) is non-different from that which is discerned, according to the principle that "it is considered non-distinct from what it is distinct from," it is established as being separate even while not being distinct from that [wisdom].
This is the *jñānadharmakāya* (wisdom-dharma-body).

Having thus described the first body, he speaks of the second—the *dharmakāya*, which consists of non-conceptual wisdom (*niṣprapañcajñāna*), is untainted (*anāsrava*), and consists of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth:
"The factors conducive to awakening, the immeasurables, the liberations in their proper sequence, the ninefold meditative attainments, and the tenfold totality. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.2)

The bases of mastery are of eight kinds according to their classification; [furthermore, there are] absence of strife, knowledge resulting from prayer, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.3)
Then there are the four purities in all their aspects, the ten masteries, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the state of having nothing to guard. Abhis 8.4.

The threefold establishment of mindfulness, the threefold nature of non-forgetfulness, the complete eradication of latent predispositions, and great compassion for living beings. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.5)
The eighteen unique qualities belonging exclusively to the Sage,
as well as the knowledge of all aspects— this is designated as the Dharma-body.
Thus, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*) range from the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the noble eightfold path.
As before, there are the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
There are two [meditations] consisting of: one who possesses form internally sees forms externally, and one who is formless internally sees forms externally.
Having personally realized with one's body the beautiful liberation and having attained it, one dwells therein—this is one;
the four [formless attainments] consisting of the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and the cessation of perception and feeling—this is one. Thus, there are eight liberations.

The nine attainments (*samāpatti*) consist of the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The tenfold totality (*kṛtsna*) consists of earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, consciousness, and space.

There is a tetrad consisting of those who, while possessing the perception of internal form or being formless internally, perceive external forms through the modes of limited or vast, and having mastered them, know them.

The fourfold [base] consisting of one who, while still possessing the perception of internal form, looks upon blue, yellow, red, and white without being overcome by them—these constitute the eightfold bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). Because it uproots the continuity of the strife of afflictions belonging to the mental streams of others, it is called "absence of strife" (*araṇā*). Because it proceeds throughout the cycle of existence even in the non-concentrated state through the fulfillment of its vow—which removes doubt and is free from attachment and obstruction regarding all signs—it is called "knowledge resulting from prayer" (*praṇidhijñāna*).

The six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), as previously mentioned, along with the four purities consisting of the purity of basis, object, mind, and knowledge—these are the four purities.
The ten masteries (*daśa vaśitā*) are: mastery over life, mind, requisites, karma, rebirth, resolve, aspiration, supernormal power, knowledge, and dharmas.
[These are added to] the ten powers (*daśa balāni*) mentioned previously.
And there are the four fearlessnesses.
The Tathāgata is one whose conduct of body, speech, and mind is completely pure; he has no contrary conduct.

That which one might think should be concealed out of fear of being fully known by others—this constitutes the threefold non-protection. In the teaching of the Dharma, toward those who wish to hear, those who do not wish to hear, and those who desire both, he dwells with mindfulness, free from attachment, aversion, and both, maintaining equanimity; thus, the application of mindfulness is threefold.
His nature of non-confusion is characterized by the non-transgression of the proper time for acting for the benefit of sentient beings.

The eradication of the latencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*), which constitute the seeds of formative impressions (*vāsanā*); the intention to benefit all beings; great compassion (*mahatī karuṇā*) toward living beings; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); and omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), the previously mentioned [qualities] such as the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) are also included.

Some maintain that the Dharma-body is designated as all the factors of enlightenment and so forth, which, through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), have undergone revolution and consist of non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*).
Others, however, [state]:
"Those untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena which have attained purity in every aspect..."
The essential body of the Sage has their own nature as its characteristic.

Having thus explained that— by accepting the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena according to their literal sense— the Svābhāvikakāya is characterized by the nature of those [phenomena], which is their non-arising (*anutpādatā*), and that this very Dharmatākāya is designated as the "Dharmakāya" through the elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); and having raised the doubt, "What then are those untainted phenomena whose characteristic nature is the Dharmakāya?", they introduce the verse beginning with "The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*)," and so forth.

How are those non-dual minds and mental factors to be accepted as necessarily existing, which—through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) by means of generating the appearance of distinguished objects according to the conventional reality of yogins—perform purposeful actions such as teaching the Dharma?
Others say they are "subsumed" (*saṅgṛhīta*);
some [say this] in the *Explanation of the Four Bodies* (*kāyacatuṣṭayavyākhyāna*).
The essential body, the enjoyment body, and likewise the other, the emanation body— the Dharma-body, together with its activity, is thus proclaimed to be fourfold.
Since the word "dharma-kāya" does not follow the word "svābhāvika" in this verse (*kārikā*), [some maintain that] there are only three bodies (*kāyatraya*).

Others, however, argue that because of the force of the purpose already demonstrated and for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse, this was stated in order to connect [the *svābhāvika* body] with the activity (*kāritra*) of gnosis itself;
therefore, there is no contradiction, and the fourfold body (*kāyacatuṣṭaya*) as explained in other sections remains valid.
To demonstrate the distinction between the concentration of non-affliction (*araṇā-samādhi*) of the Śrāvakas and others and that of the Buddha, he says in an intermediate verse:
"The non-affliction of a Śrāvaka consists in avoiding the afflictions of human beings;
the non-affliction of the Victor (*jina*) exists in villages and other places for the sake of cutting off the stream of those very afflictions. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.7)

Thus: "May no affliction arise in anyone upon seeing us"—this avoidance of the arising of afflictions in humans is the *araṇā-samādhi* (meditative concentration of non-affliction) of the Śrāvakas and others.
For the Tathāgatas, however, there is the uprooting of the entire continuity of afflictions in all beings; thus, their *araṇā-samādhi* in villages and other places is superior.
To demonstrate the distinction between the knowledge resulting from the vows (*praṇidhijñāna*) of the Śrāvakas and others and that of the Tathāgata, he says in an intermediate verse:
Effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and ever-present;
the Buddha’s knowledge of aspiration is held to be that which dispels all questions. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.8)
Thus, it functions spontaneously by virtue of being signless;
it is free from attachment to form and so forth due to the absence of adherence to real entities;
and it is unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge because of the abandonment of the afflictive obscurations and the obscurations to the knowable, together with their latent predispositions.
Because it remains throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), it is eternally abiding;
because it has attained the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), it provides answers to questions. Thus, the Tathāgata’s knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) is so designated.
For Śrāvakas and others, it is not thus, due to their contrary nature.
One might ask: "If the Dharmakāya, consisting of great compassion, remains eternally in this state, how is it that [the Lord] acts as the protector of all living beings at all times?
He provides the resolution with an intermediate verse:
Whenever and for whomever the cause has reached maturity,
that [Buddha] manifests himself to bring about whatever benefit is to be accomplished for each of them.

Thus, when the cause— consisting in the encounter with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth, which has reached full maturity through focusing upon the Buddhas and others— is present, and the seeds of previously planted roots of virtue exist, then for whichever sentient being, at whichever time, the teaching of the Dharma and so forth being performed will be beneficial for their future, the Blessed One acts for that person's welfare by fulfilling his previous vows; he performs purposeful activity in accordance with the appearance [of that being], by way of abiding in the *dharmakāya* whose nature is great compassion.

The intended meaning is that although [the Buddha] is always present like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), he does not appear as a bestower of results due to a deficiency in causes produced by the fault of one's own karma.
To address the doubt as to how this is so, he provides an illustration in an intermediate verse:
"For even when the rain-cloud pours down, the seed does not sprout."
Even upon the appearance of Buddhas, one who lacks the capacity does not enjoy the auspicious.

Thus it is said: just as when the king of gods sends down rain, seeds such as sesame that have become non-seeds due to putrefaction and the like do not sprout, so too, even upon the appearance of the Buddhas—who are skilled in fulfilling all desires—one who is unworthy does not obtain the auspicious [result], such as hearing the True Dharma (saddharma).

If it is asked: "How can the Dharmakāya, which is of the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), which resides in the substratum of the specific mental continuum of yogins, which arises at every moment, and which is all-pervading, be called eternal?"
He states this in an intermediate verse:
"Thus, because of the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervading;
and because of its very inexhaustibility, he is also called eternal. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.11)

Thus, by the very logic stated above, because the Blessed One’s capacity for performing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is extensive through the medium of manifestation in all respects, and because he abides in continuity throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), he is respectively designated as "the Buddha," "pervasive" (*vyāpin*), and "eternal" (*nitya*), due to his lack of exhaustion.
3. The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Having thus described the two bodies, the third is the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*), which has the nature of the Form Body (*rūpakāya*) and is resplendent with the primary marks and secondary signs. Regarding it, he says:
"This body of the Sage, consisting of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor signs, is considered the Enjoyment Body because of its enjoyment of the Mahāyāna. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.12)

Thus, this [body], consisting of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, is the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body) of the Blessed Buddha, because it is the enjoyment of the joy and bliss derived from the supreme, irreproachable Dharma of the Mahāyāna by the great Bodhisattvas who have entered the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
If one asks, "What are those thirty-two marks? [they are as follows:]

He speaks in five intermediate verses: "His hands are marked with wheels; his feet are like those of a tortoise; his fingers and toes are joined by a web; his hands and feet are youthful and soft; and his body is possessed of seven prominent parts. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.13)

He has long fingers, broad heels, and well-proportioned limbs; his body is expansive, straight, and marked by the *śaṅkhapada* [conch-shell mark] on the soles of his feet; his body hair grows upward; he has shanks like those of the eneya antelope, and arms that are powerful and long; and his private organs are sheathed within a recess like those of a horse. // Abhis 8.14 //

He is golden-colored with a delicate complexion; his body hairs grow singly, turning to the right; his face is marked by a tuft of hair (ūrṇā); his torso is like that of a lion; his shoulders are rounded and the space between them is well-filled. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.15)
His inferior taste is renowned as the most excellent of tastes; his body is like the circle of a banyan tree;
he has a protuberance on his head, broad and beautiful jaws, the voice of Brahmā, and very white teeth; his chin is like that of a lion. Abhis 8.16.
The teeth are equal in size, closely set, and complete in number—four sets of ten;
his eyes are blue, and his eyelashes are like those of a bull; for these are indeed the thirty-two marks. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.17)
Thus: (1) by following and rising to meet one's teachers and so forth, he has hands and feet marked with wheels;
(2) because of his firm undertaking of the vows, he has well-placed feet like those of a tortoise;
(3) by practicing the four means of attraction, he has hands and feet with fingers and toes joined by webs, like those of a royal swan.

(4) From the giving of excellent food, drink, and so forth, [he attains] the quality of having soft and youthful hands and feet. (5) From the giving of especially excellent foods to be licked and so forth, because the regions of his hands, feet, shoulders, and neck are elevated, he possesses the quality of the seven protuberances. (6) From the releasing of those condemned to death, he possesses the quality of long fingers.
(7) From the act of sustaining life, he has long heels;
(8) from abstaining from taking life, he has broad and straight limbs;
(9) from undertaking wholesome dharmas, he has high-arched feet.
(11) From increasing the undertaking of wholesome virtues already acquired, he has body hairs that grow upward;
(12) from giving knowledge, arts, and so forth with due respect, he has calves like those of the eneya antelope;
(13) from not rejecting supplicants who come seeking available goods, he has long and well-proportioned arms.
(13) Because of encouraging all people to undertake the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and guarding secret mantras, he has the private organ withdrawn into a sheath (*kośagatabastiguhyatā*).
(14) Because of giving excellent bedding and mats, he has a golden complexion (*suvarṇavarṇatā*).
(15) Because of giving excellent gifts such as palaces, he has smooth skin (*ślakṣṇacchavitā*).
(16) Because he avoided socializing and the like, his body hairs grow singly and curl to the right;
(17) because he seated all his elders in their proper places, his face is marked by a *ūrṇā* tuft of hair;
(18) because he never exhausted others with talkative speech, the upper half of his body is like that of a lion.
(19) Because of speaking kindly, uttering well-spoken words, and being compliant, there is the well-guarded shoulder-mass.
(20) From the giving of medicine and so forth, there is the fullness between the shoulders.
(21) From attending to those who are ill, there is the excellence of the sense of taste.
(22) From encouraging the construction of groves, gardens, and so forth, comes the mark of having a body as well-proportioned as a banyan tree (*nyagrodha-parimaṇḍalatā*).
(23) From the superior gift of monasteries and other such dwellings, comes the mark of having a crown protrusion on the head (*uṣṇīṣa-śiraskatā*).
(24) From speech that is gentle and so forth, comes the mark of having a broad tongue (*prabhūta-jihvatā*).
(25) From making the true Dharma known to the sentient beings of all world-systems, one attains the Brahma-voice; (26) from abstaining from frivolous speech, one attains a jaw like that of a lion;
(27) from honoring all people and so forth, one attains white teeth.
(28) Because of purity of livelihood, there is evenness of teeth;
(29) because of the practice of truthful speech, there is no gap between the teeth;
(30) because of the non-habituation to slanderous speech, there are forty teeth.
(31) From regarding all sentient beings as one’s only son, he possesses deep blue eyes;
(32) from seeing [the world] as free from hostility and the like, he possesses eyelashes like those of a cow.
He states by means of an intermediate verse that the mark is accomplished through the accomplishment of the means:
Whatever cause there may be here for the accomplishment of each respective characteristic, this [result] is the characteristic of their full attainment.
Thus, having fulfilled those specific causes which are the means of accomplishing these marks, those thirty-two marks manifest.
If one asks, "What are their causes? [the answer follows].
He states this with two intermediate verses:
"Following after the gurus and so forth, firmness regarding the vow, gathering [disciples], serving [the teacher], and the giving of excellent things. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.19)

The undertaking of releasing those condemned to death, the increase of the wholesome, and so forth—such is the cause, as stated in the sūtras, which establishes the characteristics [of the Buddha]. Abhis_8.20 //
Thus [it is said]. These two verses have already been clarified during the occasion of the explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) above;
therefore, they will not be elaborated upon again.
Having thus explained the primary characteristics, he states the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) by means of twelve intermediate verses (*antaraśloka*).
The nails and fingers of the Sage are copper-colored, glossy, and prominent; they are rounded, well-proportioned, and tapering; and his veins are hidden and without knots. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.21)
The ankles are hidden, the feet are even like those of a lion, an elephant, a twice-born bird, or a bull;
his stride is powerful, his gait is graceful to the right, and his limbs possess straightness and roundness.
Smoothness and regularity, purity and softness, cleanliness of the limbs, and the presence of the primary marks, as well as beautiful and broad circular limbs. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.23)
Evenness of gait, purity of the eyes, delicacy, the state of having limbs that are neither dejected nor over-exalted, and the state of having well-knit limbs; Abhis 8.24.
Well-proportioned limbs, purity of light undimmed by darkness, rounded, polished, unblemished eyes, a slender abdomen, and depth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.25)
The navel spirals to the right and is beautiful to behold from all sides;
his conduct is pure, and his body is free from moles or dark spots.
His hands are soft as cotton-wool; his lines are glossy, deep, and long;
his face is not overly long; and his lips are like the bimba fruit, resembling its reflection.
The tongue is soft, slender, and red; his voice has the resonance of a thundercloud;
his tone is lovely and melodious; and his fangs are rounded, sharp, white, and even. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.28)
The nose is high and gradually tapered, supremely pure;
the eyes are wide, adorned with lashes, and possess the appearance of lotus petals. Abhis 8.29.
His eyebrows and arms are long, smooth, very glossy, and possessed of even hairs;
his ears are plump, long, symmetrical, and free from any defects.
The forehead is unwrinkled; the head is broad and full; the eyebrows possess a radiant luster, are smooth, and have unconfused hair-roots. (Abhis 8.31)
The hair of men is not coarse and captivates with its fragrance;
the Śrīvatsa and the Svastika—these are considered the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) of a Buddha. Abhis 8.32.
Thus: (1) through being free from passion for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he has copper-colored nails;
(2) through his resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare of all sentient beings, he has glossy nails;
(3) through his birth in a noble lineage, he has prominent nails.
(4) Because his conduct is irreproachable, he has rounded fingers;
(5) because he has fully accumulated roots of merit, he has thick-set fingers;
(6) because he has proceeded correctly and in proper sequence, he has tapering fingers.
(7) Because his physical actions and so forth, as well as his livelihood, are well-concealed, he has concealed veins;
(8) because he severs the knots of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he has veinless [or knotless] veins;
(9) because his understanding of the Dharma is well-concealed, he has concealed ankles.
(10) He has level feet because he delivers people dwelling in all difficult places;
(11) he has the gait of a lion’s stride because he is skilled in overcoming men; (12) he has the gait of an elephant’s stride because he is skilled in overcoming elephants.
(13) Because of his skill in moving through the air, he has the gait of a swan’s stride;
(14) because of his skill as a bull among men, he has the gait of a bull’s stride;
(15) because he follows the rightward path, he has a rightward-turning gait.
(16) Graceful movement through the skill of being pleasing; (17) straight movement through constant absence of crookedness of mind; (18) well-proportioned limbs through proclaiming pure qualities.
(19) Because he has wiped away sinful qualities, his limbs are polished;
(20) because he teaches the Dharma according to the needs of those to be trained, his limbs are well-proportioned;
(21) because his conduct regarding the body and so forth is pure, his limbs are pure.
(22) Because of his compassionate mind, he has soft limbs;
(23) because of his pure mind, he has pure limbs;
(24) because of his perfected discipline of the Dharma, he has perfectly complete secondary characteristics.
(25) From proclaiming the vast and beautiful qualities [of the Dharma], he has broad and beautiful limbs; (26) from having an even mind toward all, he has even strides;
(27) from teaching the perfectly pure Dharma, he has pure eyes.

(28) From teaching the Dharma in an easily understood manner comes the quality of having delicate limbs; (29) from always possessing a mind that is never dejected comes the quality of having undejected limbs; (30) from the complete emergence of wholesome qualities comes the quality of having prominent limbs.
(31) Because he has exhausted further rebirth, his body is well-knit;
(32) because he teaches dependent origination with its well-distinguished factors, his major and minor limbs are well-proportioned;
(33) because he perceives the meaning of things with perfect purity, his light is pure and free from darkness.
(34) A well-rounded belly, due to being one who causes disciples to be endowed with virtuous conduct;
(35) a polished belly, due to having wiped away the defects of saṃsāra;
(36) an unbent belly, due to having broken the horns of pride.
(37) Because he causes the exhaustion of unwholesome states to cease, he has a non-sunken belly. (38) Because he has penetrated the profundity of the Dharma, he has a deep navel.
(39) Because he brings about disciples who grasp [the teaching] in a favorable manner, his navel curls to the right.
(40) He possesses universal loveliness because he brings about a retinue that is universally pleasing.
(41) He possesses pure conduct because his mind is pure. (42) His body is free from moles and dark spots because he has disciplined himself away from unseasonable practices.
(43) Because he teaches the Dharma that brings about lightness of body and so forth, his hands are as soft and delicate as cotton.
(44) Because he has attained the state of a great śramaṇa with a gentle nature, the lines on his palms are smooth.
(45) Because he abides in the profound Dharma, the lines on his palms are deep.
(46) Because he teaches the Dharma that is completely pure regarding its future consequences, his lines on the palms are long.
(47) Because he teaches the trainings in great abundance, his mouth is not overly long. (48) Because he knows all worlds as being like reflections, his lips are like the reflection of an image.
(49) Because he disciplines others with gentle speech, his tongue is soft; (50) because he is endowed with abundant virtues, his tongue is slender;
(51) because he disciplines the Dharma for the sake of young people who are attached and difficult to penetrate, his tongue is red.
(52) By virtue of being free from all fear, he has a voice like the thundering of clouds;
(53) by virtue of his speech being sweet and so forth, he has a voice that is sweet, lovely, and charming;
(54) by virtue of having turned away from the fetters of existence, he has rounded canine teeth.
(55) He has sharp fangs because he subdues those who are difficult to tame;
(56) he has white fangs because he disciplines through the most pure dharmas;
(57) his fangs are even because he is established in equanimity.
(58) Because he illuminates the correct sequential realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*), his canine teeth are even;
(59) because he establishes the excellence of wisdom (*prajñāprakarṣa*), his nose is prominent;
(60) because he is endowed with pure persons, his nose is clean.
(61) Because his nature is supremely noble, he has wide eyes;
(62) because he has fully gathered a multitude of sentient beings, he has eyelashes like those of a bull;
(63) because he is beloved by all young women, his eyes have lashes like the petals of white and blue lotuses.
(64) Because he perceives the long-term consequences [of actions], he has long eyebrows; (65) because he is skilled in the subtle Dharma and Vinaya, he has smooth eyebrows;
(66) because his mental continuum is wholesome and affectionate, he has very glossy eyebrows.
(67) Because he perceives faults everywhere, his eyebrows have hairs of equal length;
(68) because he averts the greatest suffering, his arms are full and long;
(69) because he has conquered the battle against passion and the like, his ears are symmetrical.

(70) Because his mental continuum is unharmed toward all sentient beings, he possesses unimpaired faculty of hearing; (71) because he is not subject to transformation by the distortions of any [wrong] views, he possesses a forehead that is not sunken;
(72) because he crushes all opponents, he possesses a broad forehead.
(73) By virtue of having fulfilled the supreme vows, he possesses the perfection of the head-hairs (*pūrṇottamāṅgatā*).
(74) By virtue of turning away from delight in sense objects, he possesses hair as dark as a bee (*bhramarasadṛśakeśatā*).
(75) By virtue of having abandoned the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation, he possesses dense hair (*citakeśatā*).
(76) Because he has fully understood the teaching with a gentle intellect, his hair is soft.
(77) Because his consciousness is not overwhelmed by passion and other defilements, his hair is not disheveled.
(78) Because he always speaks words that are not harsh, his hair is not coarse.
(79) By being strewn with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), [he has] fragrant hair;
(80) by being conducive to beauty in every respect, [he has] hands and soles of feet that are beautiful with the *śrīvatsa*, the *svastika*, and the *nandyāvarta*—
these constitute the Nirmāṇakāya.
Having thus described the three bodies, the fourth is the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body), which is common to all ordinary beings;
regarding it, he says:
"By means of which it performs various benefits for the world equally."
Until the end of existence, that emanation-body of the Sage remains uninterrupted.

Thus, that body by which—in the form of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and others—he equally accomplishes the desired welfare of sentient beings in all world-systems until the end of saṃsāra, is the emanation-body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*) of the Blessed Buddha; it is to be understood as the fourth [body], which continues in an uninterrupted succession and is common to all ordinary people. These are the activities of a Buddha.

Thus, having indicated the three conceptually constructed bodies (parikalpitakāya) in relation to gnosis and so forth—since the Buddha and others are objects manifested through the cultivation of the nature of the essential body (svābhāvikakāya)—gnosis itself, by way of producing appearances such as the enjoyment body (sāmbhogikakāya), performs purposeful action (arthakriyā) according to conventional truth. Its activity consists in appearing to those to be trained; and because it arises based on the sovereignty of that [essential body], it is indeed the dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Likewise, his karma is held to be uninterrupted as long as saṃsāra lasts;
it consists of the pacification of the realms of existence and the fourfold means of attraction. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.34)

[The application of wisdom] is directed toward settling [the mind], toward the realization of purification within affliction, toward the true nature of the welfare of sentient beings, and toward the six perfections. (Abhis 8.35)
In the Buddha-path, in emptiness by its very nature, in the cessation of duality, in conventional designation, in non-apprehension, and in the maturation of embodied beings; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.36.
Regarding the prevention of attachment to the path of a bodhisattva, the attainment of awakening, the purification of the buddha-field, and with respect to certainty; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.37.

In the immeasurable benefit of sentient beings, in qualities such as serving the Buddhas, in the factors of enlightenment, in the non-perishing of karmic actions, and in the vision of the truths; Abhis 8.38.
And regarding the abandonment of error, the method of its lack of substantial reality, purification along with its equipment, and the conditioned and the unconditioned; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.39.
The non-perception of distinctions and the establishment in nirvāṇa—this is considered the twenty-sevenfold activity of the dharmakāya. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.40)
Thus: having first performed the activity of pacifying rebirth, characterized by not abiding in attachment to auspicious or inauspicious states of existence;
having established [beings] in the four means of attraction, such as generosity;
and having awakened them through the knowledge consisting of hearing and so forth, by way of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted regarding the discordant factors and their remedies;

Like a magician, having established [beings] in the welfare of others—characterized by loving-kindness and so forth—which is free from attachment and the like, and in the true nature of the welfare of sentient beings;
subsequently, in the practice of the six perfections as manifested by the purity of the three spheres, which constitutes one's own welfare;
and immediately thereafter, on the path of the Buddha, characterized by the ten paths of wholesome action, which consists of the welfare of both self and others.
Then, through the practice of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,

and subsequently, by means of the empowerment of the perfection of generosity, he establishes [beings] in the non-dual dharma characterized by the penetration of the all-pervading dharmadhātu on the first stage;

thereafter, on the second stage and those following, he establishes them in the conventional knowledge of all dharmas, such as the perfections of ethical discipline and so forth, which serve as the cause for the fulfillment of the accumulations.

In this sequence, through the empowerment of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), on the sixth stage there is the non-apprehension of all phenomena, characterized by non-attachment to the existence of knowledge and the object of knowledge;
immediately thereafter, on the seventh stage, through the power of the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*), there is the maturation of sentient beings;
and then, on the eighth stage, through the power of the perfection of strength (*balapāramitā*), there is the bodhisattva path which is not shared with the śrāvakas and others.
Furthermore, in that very same context, upon the abandonment of all attachment to entities,

and subsequently upon the attainment of enlightenment through the power of the ninth perfection of aspiration, and immediately thereafter, having established [the practitioner] in the purification of various Buddha-fields on the tenth stage through the force of the perfection of primordial wisdom;

Furthermore, in that very same state, which consists of being bound to only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), he establishes [beings] in the certainty of perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*) and in the qualities such as approaching the Buddhas in all world-systems for the sake of sentient beings in the world-systems of the ten directions. In this sequence, he further establishes them in that very same state, which consists of the nature of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), characterized by the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) that bring about the attainment of all enlightenment.
In the non-perishing of the connection between action and its fruit,
in the realization of things as they truly are,
and in the abandonment of all perversions.
In the knowledge that abandons misconceptions devoid of objective basis;
in the purification of a bodhisattva, characterized by natural purity;
and in the equipment which is the cause for purification free from all stains.

Having established [beings] in the thorough knowledge that the conditioned and the unconditioned are non-distinct by virtue of their nature of emptiness, he settles them in the Tathāgata-stage, which is nirvāṇa.
Thus, like the Dharma-body, his twenty-sevenfold activity is intended to persist as long as saṃsāra endures; this is the *kāritra* (function).
Through the sequential explanation of the first production of the thought of awakening and the final activities, the sequence of the remaining intermediate topics should also be understood.
I have not recorded [this] here for fear of excessive length.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth chapter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
This is the explanation intended for the sake of beings with moderate inclination.

Having thus explained the *Prajñāpāramitā* by means of eight topics for the sake of benefiting sentient beings who delight in detailed exposition, he speaks again in another manner for the purpose of explanation:
"The characteristic, its application, its excellence, and its sequence."
Its culmination and its maturation—this is another sixfold summary of the subject matter. // 1 //
Thus: first, there is the definition [of the three omnisciences] as the objective basis for the three types of omniscience, beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Next, because one applies oneself to the cultivation of the three types of omniscience for the sake of mastery, there is the "application to the three omnisciences," which is the clear realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).
Then, through intense practice, there is the attainment of excellence; thus, the "culminating clear realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*) is the stage of excellence of the three types of omniscience.

Then, for the sake of reaching certainty regarding the realized object, there is the refinement of the meaning through its analysis both individually and collectively; this is the serial realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) at the stage of the sequence of the three types of omniscience.
Then, because there is no further progression toward excellence, there is the perfect awakening in a single moment (*samyagekakṣaṇābhisambodha*) at the final stage of the three types of omniscience.
Following that is its fruit.
Thus, the Dharma-body, which is the maturation of the three types of omniscience, is accompanied by its activity.
In this way, the Mother of the Victors should be explained through the sixfold summary of meaning as previously described;
this explanation is for the sake of sentient beings who take delight in concise forms.

Having explained [the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*] by means of this sixfold summary of the subject matter out of compassion for beings who delight in the intermediate [length], he now says—out of consideration for beings who delight in the concise—another way of explaining it:
"The object is threefold; the cause consists of four aspects;
the dharma-body is the fruit, and activity is another; thus is the summary of the subject matter in three ways. (2)

Thus: first, the nature of the three types of omniscience, beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), is the cause that is the object of engagement. How is that practiced? Immediately following that, the fourfold clear realization (*abhisamaya*), beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), is the practice. What is the fruit of that very object for one who practices in this way? Subsequently, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) together with its activity is the fruit. Thus, the Mother of the Victors (*jinajanani*) should be explained through these three summaries of meaning in that same manner.
Whether by way of meaning, by way of words, or even by way of synonyms for the name,
the wise should know that the summarized meaning in all the Mothers is exactly this much. // 1 //
Otherwise, there would not be a correct compendium of all [the mudrās];
therein, through the distinctions such as the *piṇḍa* and so forth, a specific excellence certainly arises. (2)
By the power of the noble Vimuktisena, the mere meaning has been shown here for easy understanding, omitting extensive verbal elaboration. (3)
Having bowed to the Guru Vairocana, who possesses the wisdom of a true preceptor, Haribhadra composes this clear commentary on the kārikās.
By whatever merit has been acquired by me through the composition of this work, may all living beings thereby attain the enlightened wisdom of the Sugata. (5)

Where am I, a man of such meager intellect, excluded from all the scriptures? And where is this meaning of the scripture, endowed with greatness and accessible only through the path of the Noble Ones? (6)
Nevertheless, even though this was outside my domain, I have exerted myself;
may the virtuous forgive me for this, as it was done solely with the intention of benefiting others.
Aha! Having been exhausted by various doctrines, I have finally, after a long time, beheld this abode of peace, the view of the Perfection of Wisdom. (8)
Thus ends the *Abhisamayālaṃkāravṛtti*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstra* composed by the master Haribhadra.
It was translated and finalized by the Indian paṇḍita Vidyākaraprabha and the great eye of the world, the venerable Śrīkūṭa;
it was subsequently thoroughly verified by the venerable paṇḍitas Amara, Gomin, and others, as well as the monk Dhīmatprajña.
